political prisoners should be distinguished from ordinary criminals, has produced an effect never contemplated by the hon. member for North East Cork. When Mrs. Montagu was removed from Dublin to Derry Gaol the " Londonderry Journal " informs its readers that "she wore her own clothes, was attired in a dress of deep mourning, and a thick veil covered her face." The same paper says : " With regard to the clothing of prisoners it may be mentioned that shortly after the O'Brien episcod a rule was passed by the Prisons Board to the effect that any prisoaer undergoing sentence nay, with the sanction of the doctor, wear his or her own clothes, provided such prisoner has suitable clothing and a sufficiency of underclothing to maintain clean- liness and comfort. It is, therefore, not improbable that Mrs. Montagu may, under this rule, obtain the sanction of the prison doctor to wear her own clothes." This is by no means the first abuse of the rule by the Castle authorities. The Belfast insur- ance swindlers were the favoured recipients of a similar concession. Mr. Balfour is determined to associate political offenders with felons alike in their privileges and in their punishment.

--- A monument to Rouget de l'lsle,the writer of the "Marseillaise" was unveiled on Sunday, by M. Gob- let, at Choisy. It was at Choisy,says our Paris Cor- respondent, that Rouget de l'lsle lived many years in poverty, and died while in receipt of £BO a year granted by Louis Philippe. The monument was or- dered and paid for by the Freemasons ot French lodges, and designed by M. Leblanc, the sculptor. The pedestal is in granite,surrounded by twelve mor- tars, held together by chains. Rouget do l'lsle's statue is in bronze, and he is supposed to be recit- ing the hymn which roused France to thrust back the Monarchical armies leagued against her. After I the ceremony, at which M. Goblet gave the history of this inspiring poem,the company went to see the I chamber in which, as an old man, Rouget de l'lsle vegetated. It is in a house in the Rue St. Elqi, now Rue Rouget de Vlsle, and is a garret, at present used as a lumber-room and for drying clothes. The fire- place has no chimneypiece. Rouget de l'lsle, tradi- non says, was neat in his person, and eked out his wretched income by writing letters forpeasants and other poor folk, and teaching music at fivepence a lesson.

" Muckle Jock, and other stories of peasant life In the north," is from the pen of the late Malcolm M`Lennan. The volume, published by Messrs. Mac- millan and Co., is a selection from two books of stories originally issued under the title of "Peasant life in the north." They created considerable istit when they first made their appearance. and we do not doubt that the issue in the present form will he heartily welcomed by all classes of readers. It should be stated of these stories that they are as striking and as vivid as photographs, and carry the impress of truth in every line. It is questionable if any work has been issued which so completely reveals village life in Scotland in its native simpli- city. No two stories can be said to be like each other, and yet there is nothing about any of them Which is in any degree strained or sensational. The shrewdness and strength of Scotch character are finely portrayed, and the mysteries of love, life, and death are dealt with it every story in a way which preserves the attention and excites the ad- miration of the reader. We have to hand in the "Golden Treasury" series, published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co., "Trial and death of Socrates," being the Eethyphron, Apology, Crito, and Phosdo of Plato, translated iato English by F. J. Church, M.A. The translator of this work has had the advantage, of course, of the labours of the men who have gone before him, but it is due to him to say that his work through- out is admirably done. The introduction is exceedingly valuable,for it not only gives practically all that is known of the career of Socrates, but a summary of and an essay upon hie writings. Indeed, no better introduction could be had to the study of the great Greek who made himself a name by his ethical teaching 400 years before the Christian era. When put upon his trial for heterodox teaching, Socrates, in the course of his defence said " Athenians. I hold you in the highest regard and love, but I will obey God rather than you," words which, it is pointed out, are strikingly parallel to those afterwards uttered by St. Peter, namely "Wei ought to obey God rather than man." The title-page contains vignette portraits of Socrates and Plato, and the volume, which is handsomely bound, is issued at 2s. ed. Another work of the same series is "The poems of Shelley, selected and arranged by Stopford A. Brooks." A century has passed since Shelley's birth, and, after much discussion, he may be said to have taken a place which he will for ever hold as one of England's greatest loets. Although frequently condemned as irreligious . his tone, he was really religious using the word in its broadest sense, and this being the case, it is refresh- ing to find the Rev. Stopforcl Brooke remarking that " There are more clergymen and more religious lay men than we imagine who trace to the emotion Shelley awakened in them when they were young their wider and better views of God." Shelley was in revolt against wrong in every form, and he was therefore an out-and-out Radical. Some of his finest poems are songs consecrated to liberty, and they did great things when they were written in stimu- lating the demand for redress of the wrongs of the people. The selections in this volume are admirably arranged, and the introduction is just and sympathetic. We can strongly commend the volume to those who can appreciate poetry of the highest order. "First lessons in business matters," is the title of an admirable little work published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co. It is written by a banker's daughter, author of "A guide to the unprotected," and is altogether a very pertinent and valuable treatise. Very few business men of experience will fail to find something even in these first lessons which will be useful to them. There is a capital index, so that reference to the text is easy. The latest story by John Strange Winter, the author of " Bootle's Baby," is styled "Mere luck." It is like the rest of her works in being pleasantly written, and full of genuine interest, and it is like some of them, too,in giving a picture cf soldier life. But this is simply an incidental feature. The main interest attaches to the fortunes of little Ted Brown, the crossing sweeper. 'I he plot is well worked out,and the story is bright and read- able from beginning to end. The publishers are Messrs. ' F. V. White and Co. "My expertences as an executioaer," by James Berry, is edited by Mr. H. Snowden Ward. The volume, published at Is.. by Messrs. Percy Lund and Co., is al- together business-like in its treatment of an extraordin- ary subject. Mr. Berry gives his experience from his first appointment up to his retirement, and certainly shows that he has paid great attention to his duties with a view to ensure their efficient performance. The frontispiece bears a portrait of Berry, and there are various portraits of men and women he has executed. Messrs. Henry Good and Son have just published in a shilling volume a revised edition of " Facts for politi- cians," by the late Mr. John Noble. The work gives a vast quantity of information, which represents an en- ormous amnunt of painstaking research and classifica- tion. It deals with many subjects which are in the front rank at the present moment; and the facts and figures advanced may in all cases be thoroughly relied upon. The Liberal politician could have no better weapon in his armoury for fighting the Tories in their gross mis- statements as to what has been done for the working- classes and as to which party deserves credit for the work. We have received a copy from Messrs. Raphael. Tuck, and Sons of the facsimile shilling edition of the Queen's letter to the nation on the occasion of the death of the Duke of Clarence and Avondale. It is a remark- able re-production of the firm handwriting of her Majesty, and is adorned by a symbolic and thoroughly artistic border, which has been especially designed by Mr. E. J. Poynter, R.A. As many as a hun- dred thousand copies have been issued as a first edition, and beyond this especial issue there are published proofs which range from 28. to five guineas per copy. The publication is in every way a credit to Messrs. Raphael, Tuck, and Sons, and it is further to their credit that the entire profits of the sale are to be devoted to the Gordon Boys' Home. A shilling souvenir is issued ef Shakespeare's histori- cal play Henry VIII., as presented at the Lyceum Theatre by Mr. Henry Irving. It contains splendid por- gaits of Mr. Irving as Cardinal Wolsey, Mr. William Terries as King Henry Bth, and Miss Ellen Terry as Queen Catherine, The illustrations of the various scenes are by Messrs. J. B. Partridge, W. Telbin, J. flarker,and E: Craven, and they are, without exception, executed in the meat artistic style. The souvenir, it should be added, is published by the "Black and White" Publishing Co. Messrs. Cassell and Co., are publishing in monthly parts, 7d. each, their "Illustrated British Ballads." When complete the work will contain no fewer than 300 original illustrations from artists of the highest class. Every period and every style of ballad writing will be presented, including English, Welsh, Scottish, and Irish ballads, and, as the illustrations are as beautiful as they are spirited, it is a matter of course, to say that the work will be ef a unique kind. The editor is Mr. George Barnett Smith, who can:be relied upon for care in She production of an accurate text. The first part has for frontispiece a really charming etching from the picture by Gow of a scene from "The braes of Yarrow." • " Cassell's Magazine" for April contains two complete as well as portions of serial stories, besides the usual number of interesting and admirably illustrated miscel- laneous papers, amongst which may be mentioned "Colonists in embryo" ; "Concerning the standards"; "Cloud-land " ; "Chit-chat on dress"; and "The gatherer." The frontispiece of the " Quiver " is a reproduction of a striking drawing by Percy Tarrant, bearing the title "Our silver wedding." The first paper is devoted to " Some interesting Swedish institutions," followed by " Housing the homeless," " A Chinese seeker after truth," "The lessons of Spring," "Some curious chairs In our ancient churches," &c. There is a full supply, as usual, of healthy and brightly written fiction. '" Little Folks" is adorned this month with a coloured frontispiece of a little girl in quaint array. The serial stories are " The next door house," by Mrs. Molesworth, and" Through snow and sunshine, by Henry Frith. There are, of course, numerous short stories and sketches, all of them cleverly illustrated, and from" The , editor's pocket book issue many good things, as from a magic box. " The old story," which means the story of love,is the title of the etching which forms the frontispiece of the "Magazine of Art." It is from a painting by Alma Tadema, and the etching is a wonderfully fine one. The first paper is devoted to Stanhope A. Forbes, A.R.A. It is accompanied with a portrait of the artist, and repro- ductions of two of his more famous paintings, "Health to lie bride," and "By order of the Court." A not less interesting paper is written upon Sir George Reid, P.R. S.A., by Professor Baldwin Brown, and this is adorned by reproductions of his most famous portraits and paint- ings. The subjects of other illustrated papers are, " Art treasures of the Conedie Francaise," " Irish

Pending the opportunity of carrying a measure involving the principle of one man one vote, Sir William Harcourt has assisted in drafting a Bill providing that no person shall vote at Parliamen- tary elections in more than one electorial area dur- ing the period for which a given register of Parlia- mentary voters is in force. The Bill is backed by Sir George Trevelyan, Sir Horace Davey, Mr. Stens- feld, Mr. Shaw Lefevre, Hr. Broadhurst, and Mr. Asquith.

Mr. Jackson left for Dublin on the evening of the adjournment of the House. He has in the interim visited Galway with a view to aiding in the de- velopment of the mackerel fishing, and Sir John Gorst has been in the West of Ireland inspecting the light railways and the other relief works. Neither of these officials have, however, been ac- companied by a cohort of reporters. They have been engaged in practical work, and have not at- tempted any theatrical tour.

The Easter Vacation has been signalise i by the I presence in Ireland of many prominent members of the Ministry. Mr. Goschen went over to Dub- lin, and spent a day or two in the Royal Hospital, Kilmainham, with Lord and Lady Wolseley. Mr. Goschen afterwards proceeded from Dublin to Fer- neoy on a visit to his son-in-law, the Hon. Alexis Burke-Roche, a brother of Lord Fermoy. Mr. Burke- Roche married Mr. Goschen's eldest daughter on 24th April, 1882—just three years ago.

A Women's Training School at St. Louis happily combines work and play. A violet party belongs to the latter category, as well as a candy-pulling, intended for the children and the young men and girls. A committee of young ladies are to make all the arrangements. In addition to the short- hand, type-writing, and sewing classes, others for learning cookery have now been established, at which lessons are given in such national dishes as cranberry sauce, sweet potatoes, backed ham, chicken salad, and cold slaw.

Mr. Alfred Deakin, one of the counsel entruste d with the defence of Deeming in Melbourne; is the subject of an amusing anecdote. Before he entered on political life he was a leader writer on a paper that, to put it mildly, had a reputation for not be- ing enthusiastically devoted to the championship of truth. The story goes that an Irish humorist, meeting the proprietor of this paper one day, inno- cently inquired "Don't you think you ought to have something higher tan a deacon in your office? It seems to me you want a bishop on your staff." "A bishop! " cried the astonished newspaper owner; why so?" "Because you know, your statements are so sadly in need of eonfirmation."

There is no picture this year at the Royal Acad- emy that will make a sensation. The French Leighton, Monsieur Bouguereau, has a picture on the line in the big room. Mdlle. Bilinska (a Polish artist, living in Paris) sends a clever portrait of herself. Miss E. Deane a few years ago made a hit by her portrait of Anna Bilinska, which was hung on the line, and then attracted much attention. It certainly was not flattering. Now the public will be able to see how the artist has rendered herself, Another foreigner, Anna Nordgren, has a picture of a little girl dreaming by the fireside. This lady is better represented at the New Gallery by a picture ,of a peasant woman with hor child fast asleep in her arms.

Mr. Lewis Pelly, writes a correspondent, was physically one of the smallest men in the House of Commons. His carriage was, however, singularly erect, and lie was so well proportioned that his deficiency in stature was only apparent when he stood at the bar of the House hesule other men. His face was actually tanned by Eastern suns, and a I red necktie which he habitually wore when in morn- ing dress, set off his dark eyes and somewhat swarthy features and emphasised his Oriental appearance. Sir Lewis was scrupulously neat in his dress and methodical in his habits. Retold one I of his acquaintances within the last few days that I he made it a point to wear glasses when smoking so as to protect his eyes from the tobacco fumes.

Mr. Balfour gave another proof on Monday night of his keen sensibility to ridicule. The lively Dr Tanner, on a sudden impulse, moved an amendment when the Indian Councils Bill was in Committee framed on the model of the famous "put them in the dock "clause of the Irish Local Government Bill. A much duller joke would have amused the somewhat lethargic House, which laughed con- sumedly—the merriment being increased by Dr Tanner's well-feigned air of disappointment on Mr. Courtney ruling his amendment out of order. Mr. Balfour, however, who saw in the Doctor's joke a : reflection on his own statesmanship, looked as chagrined as on the day when Mr. Sexton helped hilt to couch the motion for Da Cobain's expulsion 1 in " decent English."

Sir James Allport, whose death occurred on Mon- day, at the Midland Grand Hotel, could boast of a longer connection with railways than any other pro- minent man in tne country except Mr. Samuel Laing. Be commenced his long life as a lamp-room porter, and acted ler some years as a signalman be- fore he got his opportunity. Sir James was succes- sively manager of the old Birmingham and Derby Railway, the 1 ork, Newcastle, and Berwick line, 1, which is now the North Eastern, and the Manches- ter, Sheffield, and Lincoln, before taking up his position in 1858 as manager of the Midland. It I was due to his liberal ideas that the Midland Com- pany was the first to run third-class carriages with all trains, and to abolish second-class. Ile resigned lin 1880, the directors making their estimation of ; his services by a gift of £lO,OOO, a costly service of plate, and a seat on the board.

How Dickens felt when he was about to begin a new story is described by him in a letter to Leigh Hunt, published in "The Cornhill " article. It is dated Friday, 4th May, 1855, a time when he had just finished "[lard Times," which appeared in "Household Words," and was preparing to com- mence "Little Dorrit " : " I am now (he writes) to boot, in the wandering, unsettled, restless, uncon- trellable state of being about to. begin a new a new book. At such a time lam as infirm of purpose as Macbeth, as errant as Mad Tom, and as rugged as Timon. I sit down to work, do nothiEg, get up and walk a dozen miles, come back and sit down again next day, again do nothing and get up, go down a railroad, find a place where I resolve to stay for a month; come home next morning, go strolling about for hours and hours, reject all engagements to have my time to myself, get tired of myself, and yet can't come out of myself to be pleasant to any, body else."

Lady Be— - , .....cy aoMatlef, VAC has returned to in I land after her temperance campaign in the States, is one of the few English women who can speak ateli in public. Whether it is feminine nature to be over-earnest, or whether it is only the hyper- enthusiastic woman who will come forward in this way, the fact remains that the oratorical displays of the fairer sex are usually marked with a super- abundance of seriousness, verging closely upon intensity of a painfully impressive kind, and a lack of the lighter modes of rhetoric that are every bit as powert ul, if not more so than gravity. Mr. Bese,nt and Dr. Garrett Anderson know well the require- ments of platform addresses; the former is a born 1 orator, fully aware of the singularly wide resources a speaker may make use of; the latter v lesseloquent but none the less arrestive, owing to the extreme repose of manner that she affects and her very well-modulated voice. The Countess of Jersey is a nervous but attractive speaker, albeit full of intensity.

BY LILLIAS WASSERMAN, Author of" Some Fisher Folk," " Judith," " Where , the North Wind Blows," dec., &o

CHAPTER XXXVL s _ TEDDY IN DAWGEIt. When this hope of rescue, which had been so strong for a while, died out, the reaction set in, in the form of a dull, apathetic despair. There was now no help possible for the poor men. Bill's heroic attempt to reach the shore with a rope had ended in failure; and also probably in his own destruction. Some of the fishermen had extemporised a litter from a few planks, fastened together with rope; some coats and women's shawls being gladly offere for the purpose; and had carried him away to the nearest house; a house which strangely enough happened to be occupied by the widow of the coast- , guardman who had met with such a tragic fate a short time before. Bill was quite unconscious yet; and Lady Callerley, who still maintained her post at the foot of the cliffs, caught a glimpse of his white tamp and drew back, shuddering and horror- stricken. "Bell, Bell, tell me, for I dare not look, is it my brother ?" The fisher girl, to whom she clung for support, shuddered too from head to foot, but did not answer. "Bell, why don't you speak, is it my brother, my poor, darling, brother Teddy ?" Bell put aside the clinging hands, and moved forward to the side of the rude litter. Then she turned her head over her shoulder and answered in a deep, sad voice. "Be content. It is net your brother, Lady Calletrlesr—it is mine I" ‘,l very enaracLeristic of the girl that, eves at this moment of supreme agony, she made AO great outcry, gave voice to no hysterical expres- :llollA of her own suffering. Her grief was too intense, too crushing for any outward expression of it to he possible—at least at the moment. When the sad procession had fought its way up to the heights above, all eyes were turned again issdmi the Bonny Bess. Alas, the sea had not been idle during the last few minutes The heavy cannonades had produced their due caet. A breach was now to be seen in the sides of the sloop, and the water poured through her, as through a sieve. The little black (lots cluster- ing on the after part of the deck were fewer in number, for some had been washed from their hold, :tad sucked down under the boiling surf. If noth- ing more could be done to reach them, the fate of the rest was also sealed. The sloop was breaking

up fast. Sir Lancelot Callerley had been standing near to the place where his wife was at the time when she appealed to Bell as to the fate of her brother. He had recognised her before she spoke, in fact had done so while Jack Breamish was with her, spite of her disguising shawl, and of the pale twilight. When she clung to the young fellow in her dire distress and despair, he noted it ; and though he could not hear the words that passed between them, he, watching narrowly, saw Jack hold. her hand and look down at her in a very tender fashion; then Sir Lancelot, turning away, ground his teeth with anger. But now she was alone, and her plaintive words were not altogether lost upon Sir Lancelot. If she could not love him, at least he would show her that he would dare more for her sake, and for the ease- ment of her anxiety than that young popinjay admirer of hers was likely to do !. He scrambled back to the point, and began rapidly divesting him- self of his outer garments. Some of the men, apprehending what he was about to do, tried to dissuade him from the attempt, but to their remon- strances he paid no heed whatever. "-I used to be a fair swimmer, though now in all probability a trifle out of practice !' he. said, as he adjusted a rope beneath his armpits, and gave those about him directions how toproceed, "At any rate it is worth a trial." Sir Lancelot was a powerfully made man, with a big chest and well developed muscles; but when he had been in the water a few minutes, it was evident that his work was cut out for him; and I that it would take all his powers to make much headway against the strong current. Bill had failed, with the wind and the tide in his favour, and only the cross and opposing seas to contend with.; but in the case of adventuring, as the baronet did, from the shore, instead of towards it, these advantages were reversed. Besides, as Sir Lancelot had truly. said, he was a trifle out of practice, and mere than. a trifle older since he had last attempted such a venturous feat as swimming across to Death's Ribs against a heavy sea, and in the. teeth of a nor-easter. It was a. slow progress, and before he got half the distance, the sloop parted amidships; and half of her sank back into the ocean with those of her crew who were Mahe after part.. A groan went up from the shore, answered by a few despairing yells; and then. nothing more was • audible, but the shriek of the, tempest and the thunder and hissing of the waves.. Sir Lancelot hoard the dismal groan and it struck a chill into his soul.. He was well-nigh spent. Buffeted., and stunned, and bruised, he struggled onwards, in the desperate hope that there might perchance be some left alive to, whom he would be able to bring relief:. He knew lie was gaining ground, because he could now catch the sound of I the breakers on the far side of the reef. He reckoned that the nearer he got to the rocks the More shelter he would receive; and he had no manner of doubt that comparatively smooth water awaited him, if once he were. through the sweep which kept swirling round, with such tremendous force from the open sea. But how to avoid being swept back by the mad whirling mass ofi water—that was the questionaliat troubled him.'a There was nothing for it but to watch' for an , opportunity. Wait until one wave had passed, and then dive and swim under, before the, next had time to follow. This resolution gave.libri time to breathe, mul. to, prepare for the effort;. and this was perhaps the best thing, that could., have happened, as he was. completely- exhausted by this time. It was ccam partitive rest to keep.himself himself 41,,0at, andaot lbse ground.. Then after a littitatime he braced himself fertile: final struggle; and' immediately tho.rush ,went.by,, dived under, and, struck boldly out. The time seemed interminable to those onshore who, as well as the fading lights would allow them, were anxiously watching his pi-egress • before the.] black speck, w.hich they knew to ,be his head,, as peered again heyoed the breakers; but, it was ut , reality a very short period, at most about &minute and a half. After that, it was pretty e.asy for the swimmer to gain the rocks; though he was then so worn out, that the effort of dragging himself out of the water was beyond his staength ; and he, simply chmg theire, bolding on; and panting. At last, however, he did manage io scramble up, and sat down to recover breath, before even, looking to- wards tho scene of the wrack. During the next few moments he could not pos- ed:4y have moved hand or foot, even though one of those breakers pounding away at the sloop had broken over his restiag place, and overwhelmed him? There is only a, certain amount of endurance , possible to the strongest human, being, and Sir Lancelot had come tis the limit, of his. And yet he recognised that there was no time to lose. The tide was making fast, and before long, "Death's Ribs" veauld be under water. He was stunned and bruised and bleeding; huh when 'he remembered this, be pulled himself te- gether, and began to scramble on his hands and knees over the slippery surface of the reef. He was iltin WO feeble, to withstand the force of the isinl4 which he would have encountered fully if upright, .and besides this mode of progression was much the easiest over the foam-covered rocks. When he was half-way across, he began to won- der, and think it strange that no sign of theßonny Bess was as yet visible. Could it be that his sight was failing him, or was impared by weakness? He peered anxiously through the twilight. Surely that was where she stru:k, that high pinnaeled rock yonder? He remembered noticing it and thinking how frequently that particular rock had proved fatal to ships. Great Heavens! Had the short time—for though to him it appeared a month, so hard had been the fighting—yet he knew that it must in reality onl be a short space of time,y since he saw the wreck from the shore, sufficed to break it up so thoroughly that no trace of it remained, save the few floating spars and barrels, which he could dimly discern, tossing hither and thither upon the waves? It seemed incredible, but it was a sadfact never- theless. Had all his toil and trouble—like that of poor Bill—been wasted then? _ , .._u 501

div.head: G. HUBI NEWCOMBE.
div.p: G. HUBI NEWCOMBE.

" The Lyric Author, Advertiser's and Composer's Magazine "for April contains a portrait and notice of Mrs. Newcombe, who now resides at Penketh. The chief object of the magazine is to enable song writers to place their writings before composers. Mrs. Newcombe is a prolific song writer, the cur- rent issue containing as many as ten of her lyrics. The biographic sketch is as follows We have much pleasure in publishing the repro- duction of a photograph of G. Elubi Newcombe, the popular composer, and writer of some hundreds of Lyrics. It may possibly be a surprise to many familar with this lady's work to learn that G. Huhi Newcombe is not a gentleman. Indeed, the Editor of this paper corresponded with her regu- larly for some months before he discovered that she was scarcely entitled to be designated "Esquire." Mrs. Newcombe, by Ihe way, showed her appreciation of the joke by enduring the situa- tion fur a time, and then suddenly startling the Editor, with an intimation that her son—but I am not going to print a clue to a lady's age. That Mrs. Newcombe is very young of heart will be evident to every composer who has set her charmiag love songs, and to every singer of them. Mrs. Newcombe is a Londoner, though for some time she has resided near Warrington, officiating as organist of Latchford Parish Church until ill- health compelled her to resign that position; for, unfortunately, she has been a great sufferer. Dur- ing three years she scarcely moved from the sofa on which she lay, and had to be carried upstairs and down. Her work, however, reveals nothing of her bodily weakness. The spirit is unconquerable. The amount of work she gets through will be evid- ent from the fact that she has sold more than 200 Lyrics during the last three years, in addition to the numerous songs which she has composed and published. As with most musicians,her bent showed itself at an early age. Her favourite instrument is the organ. It is just a matter of opinion as to the class of song in which she excels. The Lyric on page 4; " Deliver or die " is a capital specimen of the robust baritone, or bass song. Mrs. Newcombe has written scores as effective, many of them not the least like the work of a lady. We instance " Sir Roger," set by Gerara Cobb, " The King's Jester " (Cobb), " The Pirate," (Spawforth), " Jack Tar," ' (St. geentin), " Spirit of the Deep," (Dauber t), " King Death "(Motile), etc.

div.head: WOODEN BELL OF RIPON. OR HOW THE DEAN RAISED THE WIND.
div.p: THE WOODEN BELL OF RIPON. OR HOW THE DEAN RAISED THE WIND.

Near the railway station at Ripon is a quaint block of old almhouses with an ancient chapel dedi- cated to St. Mary Magdalen, of grey stone, backed by a grove of elms. The little chapel contains some curious wood carving, the original stone altar, and a large oak chest,in which reposes a solitary curiosity —a wooden bell, painted grey-green. The chapel is, fortunately, unrestored, left in its picturesque anti- quity to moulder away. Any one who hail seen the chapel of Barden Tower some years ago, and what it has become under the hand of the restorer, will know what it is to be giatefal that a venerable relic of antiquity has not been furbished up to suit modern taste. That St. Mary Magdalen 's would have fallen into bad hands had it been given over to restoration, may be judged by the hideous new chapel which the authorities have recently erected close to the almshouses. By that wooden bell in the oaken chest hangs a tale. In the time of our grandfathers, Dr. Waddilove was Dean of Ripon, a divine of the old port wine- drinking school. Now St. Mary Magdalen's chapel was no longer used. By the ancient endowment there was to be a resident chaplain and daily service in the little church, which the inmates of the alm- boners were expected to attend. But the chap- laincy and its emoluments were usually held by one of the canons of the Minster. The stipend went into hie pocket ; the duties were neglected. If the old almsfolk wished to pray to God daily, they might totter three-quarters of a mile up to the Minster. Dean Waidilove took on himself the chap- laincy, that is, he appropriated to the stocking of his cellar the money bequeathed to the almonership of the Magdalen Hospital. But his cellar fell low. The Dean wanted money ; his credit with the wine merchants was as low as his cellar. How was money to be raised ? One day he had the bell of the Magdalen Chapel removed from the gable in which it had hung for many centuries,and had hung silent for many years. It was an ancient bell with a Lombardic inscrip- tion :

Sum ego pulsate Rosa mundi.vocata. The bell went to the founder's ;the money paid for it went to the wino merchant, and a hamper of fine old crusted port arrived at the deanery, But Ripon people, though long-suffering, could not quite endure the" robbing of churches." Murmurs were heard; the Dean was remonstrated with. He puffed out, turning as red as a turkey cock : "Well, well! the bell shall _go. back again." And sure

enough next week the bell was seen ones more hanging in the gable of St. Mary Magdalen's chapel as of yore. The Ripon people were content. The bell was never rung, but to that they were accustomed. Who cared whether the old goodies in the hospital were ministered to or not? It was no affair of theirs if the founder's wishes were set at nought. and the walls of the Magdalen never sounded with the voice of prayer. But next spring, as on many a former one, the swallows built their nests among the eaves, and found a place about the altar of God's deserted hcuse, as they had done in. the days of the Psalm- ist. When nesting-time came, some boys began climbing about the roofs in guest of eggs. One of them, seeing a rope dungling from the bell, caught it, and began to pull, when, to his amazement, the hell uttered no sound. He crept under it. There was no clapper; and what was more, it hardly looked hollow. His curiosity was exited, and he climbed up to it and discovered that the bell was only a piece of deal turned, and painted the colour of hell-metal ! The story sounded further than ever had the old hell ; and for very shame the Dean was obliged to take it down and hide it in the chest of the Mag- dalene chapel. Autumn case round. The Dean had notable es- palliers in his garden. His trees were too attrac- tive to the urchins of Ripon to escape visits. This highly incensed the Dean, and one night hearing the boys at his apple trees, he rushed, stick in band, upon then. One he caught' by the soruff of his neck. The others Red over the wall. "Oh, you young ruffian! you audacious young scoundrel !" roared the Dean : "Where do you think thieves will go to hereafter? Whao do you think will happen to them here ?" " Please, sir ! please, sir !-- " Ilold your wicked tongue., you rascal !" thundered the Dean, whistling his cudgel round his head; " shall thrash you unmercifully now, and lock yon up in the black hole to-night, and take you to the magistrate to-morrow, and have you sent to prison. And then, if you go on with. your etealings, sir! you will go—there!' And the Dean progged with his stick in the direction of the centre of the globe. Then he-shook the boy furi- ously—" one, two," bang came the stick down. "Please, mercy, Mr. Dean -spare MO" "Spare you, sir I no—three." "But, please, Mr. Dean, my father made the wooden bell fir you," "Go along, you rascal," gasped the Dean, relaxing his hold, and rushing back into his house.—" York- shire Oddities." By S. Baring Gould, M.A.

'resiga bar), to the inevitable, for that neither he anyohe else could now manage to save her brother? Would to God that he might have died

in the place of poor Teddy ! Teddy who was loved so dearly, and for whose loss Silvia would be inconsolable. If it were only he, her husband, who had died, it would not have mattered; though then, perhaps —who knows—she might have given to his memory * tear or two ? His death would leave her free. That stinging thought did what nothing else seemed able to do, it roused Sir Lancelot from the lethargy creeping over him, and determined him, if possible, not to die. Silvia did not love him, but he would not willingly set her free. He felt the rope about his body, and laughed, even in the midst of the storm, and with the sad thought of his drowning fellow creatures fresh in his mind—laughed aloud, to think that the afore- mentioned rope assured his safety. Jealousy is said to be cruel as the grave. This is surely a libel upon the grave, which as often as not is kind ex- ceedingly. Does it not cover failure, hide disgrace, rest weariness, equalise rank, and put an end to pain? But jealousy? Is it ever accountable for one good or one noble action? Sir Lancelot was by nature generous, large- hearted, and unsuspicious. This noble passion was gradually transforming him into a mean_ selfish. Irritable person; in fact to put it concisely, into the sort of person capable of that laugh of his at the idea of thwarting somebody, even in the face of a great tragedy. At the very time when Sir Lancelot was hugging himself with the assurance of his own safety, Lady Callerley had become aware for the first time of the great risk he was encountering. Left alone, after Bell had followed those who bore away her brother's unconscious form, the suspense became unbearable to Silvia,; and she gravitated towards the group oi people at the point. A silence fell upon them as she approached, and their significant and pitting looks were not lost upon her. The clothes Sir Lancelot had thrown off when he ventured out, were lying in a heap under a rock, and Jack Brearnish, who was there also, stepped quickly in front, so that she might not see them. But it Valli impossible that she should not notice the stir, the suppressed agitation, all about

her. "What is it ?-0h; what terrible thing has hap- pened now ?" she cried, looking_froni one to another, in helpless, wondering dread, "Cousin Jack, you are hiding something from me If he was so ready witted as to endeavour to keep her from seeing those tell-tale garments, he was yet not sufficiently skilled in deceit to drive all traces of confusion fromtiaface ; and in another moment she had glided behind, him, and knew what he would fain have hidden. "My husband's coat." She said slowty, and in a bewildered sort of. way; "then whero—? Oh, Lancelot, you are not drowned, too? Lancelot, husband, come back, oonie back I Dearest, come back, or let me die with you.l'" But Sir Lancelot, as before, stated; had' no inten- sion of dying. It' would no doubt have been a 'heroic ending, but,. be, was not in any humeur for heroics. Now that he liferrested'and reconnoitre:l4lßa°, with the conclusion that he could do no-good by staying he was quite prepared to give the signal, and be drawn on shore.. But before he left the outer edge of the reef; he scanned it carefully once more, to see if by any fortunate chance some of the crew had been thrown upon,, or managed to land there. But the break' up had apparently. been too rapid, even for that, and nothing was now to he seen of the Bonny Bess but a chaotic mass of wreckage. Stay—what waathattjust below him.?. Lodged in a crevice, as though, thrown. there ,by some mighty wave, he could make- out something dark, that looked not unlike the outline ofs-human body. With considerable difficulty he clambered down the'steep face' of , the. rock, and, stood, beside the crevice. What.nfortunate chance was this! The unconscious fellowereature lying wedged in between the rocks, was: no other than Teddy—the dearly- loved brother of .Silvian. If he were notideacLalready, the' tide now rising so rapidly would have certainly drowned him ere long. He had been lashed to a spar,. as a precau- tionary measure by. Bill Widdringtom and this had evidently stood him, in good stead,,and saved him from the fate of thoothers. Sir Lancelot, stooped and bid' his hand upon Teddy s side; to,filid out whether his heart still beat or no. He could not be quite certain, but fancied that he could yet feel a faint pulsation. At any rate; whether dead or no.; the poor boy would not be... left, to the mercy of the merciless waves. He, the_husband she did.not love, should bring back the brother she did. He had recovered his strength now; and accomplished pretty easily the task.oi_carryjng the inanimate, form back over the reef.. Teddy' was ,asei small and light, of figure that he weighed' little more than a child; and indeed appeared, as case, in the big., brawny arms of his brother-in-lam'. ' Then. Sir. Lancelot removed', the rope from his own' body,. toad, fastened it around Teddy ' • and 'holding: eati to 4. and swimming bide him, made very,,good progress landward.. A ringing; cheer went up,, as, the two were at length. drawn, ashore. CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT -WARRINGTON.— - -- On Monday evening I largely:attended meeting was held in the Public Hell, Warrington, in support of the candidature of Mr. R. Pierpoint, the Pongee- , vative candidate for the borough. Mr. R. Davies presided, and amongst those on the platform were Dr. Renton], M.P. for East Down, Mr. R. Pierpoint, Major Pickmere, Alderman Francomb, Mr. John White, Mr. W. IL Bleckley; Mr. Gilbert Greens'', Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, &c. The CHAIRMAN, in his remarks, said that although they had not with him the good old baronet, they bad in his place a Warrington man, born and bred and second to none in his good wishes for the welfare of them. (Applause.) He would ray a word or two upon a ques- tion which had been raised lately by Dr. Houston, and that was the question of "Tory beer." He was very sorry indeed that Dr. Houston had gone out of his way to revive that old calumny. Dr. Houston ought to know as a lawyer that the gift of a single glass of beer would vitiate that election, and he ought to give them credit for-morncommonsense than to think they should jeopar- dise the result by such a dangerous and foolish process. (flear,ilear.) But in politics he did not believe in lying still to be kicked. He thought he would make a little inquiry in the town as to the conduct and management of that centre ot Liberal. light, the Liberal Club in I3ewsey-Btreet. He appealed to a man who knew War- rington very well, and he assured hie.' that he had seen barrels with the treble X—an alphabetical combination which he ventured to say was quite as well understood by the Liberals as by the Tones—entering the doors of that establishment. (Hear, hear, and . laughter.) He found also' when he came to examine the list of candida- tes for the forthcoming election, that in the Liberal list there were actually more brewers arid persons connected with the brewing trade coming forward on the Liberal side than on the Tory side. (Hear, hear,) All he had to say was that those who lived in glass houses should 'never throw stones. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr..',loun Warn then proposed a resolution, and explained that it was proposed at that period of the evening because it was thought that the audience might *be so inebriated by what they Would hear later on that they could not stand any sober reasoning. The resolu- tion was to the effect that, lathe opinion of that meeting the intereste of Warrington ought to be attended to by one who was thoroughly acquainted with the habits and feelings and requirements of its people, and it also adverted to Mr. Pierpoint's great ability and patriotic desire to farther the interests of his native town and countryeand pledged the meeting to support his candida, tare. Speaking of the two candidates, Mr. White said one was ant:lrish 'Home Ruler, a man Who had never been heardoef in this town at all till a few weeks ago. Healid notsay a word against Dr. Houston. Ile had a perfect right-to come to contest the borough if he chose. The king of the Cannibal Islanda, if he came and settled in this country, could, if he liked, offer himself for the borough of lArmrington. (Hear, hear and lauehter.) He was, howeveraeurprised that their Liberal friends went out cf their way to choose a stranger to come forward as their candidate. He thought their experience of 1886 woel/41 have convinced them that no stranger would havekiehance. (Hear, hear and applause.) 'Alderman FitAaTeOXB seconded the resolution moved by Mr. White. Mr. 311. PIROMINT, who was received with loud ap- plause, said he almost regretted the time when he AU in astcte of greater freedom and less responsibility,and was speaking onbehalf of hie good old frier:W..Bh. Gil- bert 'threanall, and on behalf of other members of Par- Moment. Re hadhe.ard since became back to Warring- 'ton, that he had been loolred upon as having beenetWay ler along time. 'He was happy to think that he. had .came bank to old Warrington fit to light and Wending to do it. (Applause.) He had given 'his opponent an opportunity to findalis way about the unknown toWn— (laugh ter)—he had given hi, m the opportunity of making the acquaittance of eome of them:; and he had, furthee, given him the opportunia r of being photographed. (Laughter) He hadamen on aof Or. Houston's photo- graphs, and he itook I ease to say that he was by appearance al thor, auger gentleman. (Hear, hear) He understocd on good authority that besides the ,photograph wl tick 'he had seen, Dr. Houston had been photegrap lied in other costumes. He understood that 'lre had b eon photographed as a Queen's Counsel and ass. Maste r of Arts or a Doctor of Law. He (Mr. Pierpoint) con termed that he was not fond of itavingaris photograph taken, but, ehould it be necessary, besides that picture reach had already been reproduced, he might be taken as a Master of Arts of Oxford, mad, what he reckoned veal go 'further with them, he could, if he would, be photographed in the I uniform of the Warrington Volunt seas. (Applause) It seemed to him that, if his opponei Xasaire ambitious of ' a seat as parliament, he might ha we thought of some of the 86 Home Rule seats in Jr &mad,' for which he seemed to be pmerainently quali free. (Hem, hear.) Mr. Pierpoint then went on lo mention that , just as he was coming into t, 'to 'room 'he had receivel a letter from a working-m an asking him to answer a number of questions. He w 'at' not prepared to answer all these questions on so short a notice but he would answer two of them. One was bathe effect that, if he were cleated to Parliament, would 'ire' vote for the payment of members of Parliament (cri, esof ".Yei" and a' No," and some disturbance). Most decidedly .not— •applause)—because he was not willing to it a :large amount of taxation on the country to h wee work per- formed which could be done for nothingi Hear, bear.) The next question was, would he use his weiuence and vote for the law of "one man one vote." Wes, suppos- ing that it was coupled at the same time wi tit.% thorssigh redistribution of seats. (Hear, hear and rip hum) He wished to assure them that he would not eaeglectsthe other questions, but lie did not wish to ar lower them straight off-hand. (Applause) Dr. lbsorront, who was received with lom LAPPlainkl, remarked at the outset of his Speech, on the aotrabea of ladies who were present, and criticised Mr. (.1 55t040:a attitude with regard to Women's Franchise. ItYIV Was it, he said, that Mr. Gladstone objected to it? 'lt war because the women of this country were rename 'ably in- I telligent, and nearly every one of them voted C. saservaa tive. (Laughter.) If Mr. Gladstone thought lawmen would vote Liberal there would be no man athe country more fond of giving them the franchis .0: HO wanted CO prove to them the absolute intelliga tDe of women. He was a candidate for the London c aunty' Council. There were 11,000 voters in the divisir in, of I whom 1,200 were I women, and as fir as they km we or could find out, every solitary woman that cam 0 to the poll voted for him. (Laughter.) Besides, let t Item be logical. If women were not ' fit 'to vnte t hen they were not fit to canvass, nor to try to drag tt. ir husbands by the head and shoulder into Parliama (Hear, hear and laughter.) They had at the prese at time a candidate before them who, as Mr. Pierpoint salt it, was a gentleman. ,He was a gentleman, an excellent, gentleman, for he was an Irishman. (Laughter.) Be •I sides, he was a gentleman by Art of Parliament, for he I was a lawyer. (Laughter.) Therefore, the point as to his being a gentleman was beyond doubt, but was he fit to represent an English constituency? (Cries Of "No?' and "Yes.") Why in the first place they coeld not pronounce his name. The name was not " Howston" 1 or "Hooston " but " Huiston." Having alluded to the ' part played in the election by Mrs. Houston,Dr. Rentoul strongly declared himself against the payment of members of Parliament. He said that two-thirde of the present members would not go to Parliament if it were a paid job. They went to Parliament for the honnua of going .there. If there was any intelligent workingman in a constituency who ought to be in Parliament it would take several thousands of electors to vote him there, and what was the patriotism of those electors worth if they would not subscribe a shilling a year each to support their member. He added that it would cost nearly £250,000 a year to pay each member of Parliament £1 a day, and that by receiving this money they would be pauperised. (At this point there were loud cries from the hack of the hall of " What about America ?" " What about the Ministers ?") was the whole country to be rated in order that paid paupers might be sent down to the House of Commons? There I were cries of dissent and some interruption at this point, and some one shouted out "Abolish royalties." Dr. Ren- tool seemed to think that this meant abolishing the Royal Family, and he was. entering into an argument to ,show that the Royal Family, from Henry of Battenburg and the babies' requisites upwards, onlY cost.l 100. in every £lOO of the na,donal earnings,l when some one in the audience corrected him by shouting out" Mining royalties." Dr. Rentoul confessed' that that was another question which be should not Cuter into. There being some derisive cries of" oh. oh" on his saying this, he exclaimed," Do I pretend to know everything ? I am not a Radical." His friends then came to his help with some cheering, but on his again attempting to proceed he was interrupted with Bach cries as "What about ground rents ?" Ere then informed his audience that he had a certain time to speak and if he had not then finished his speech he should sit down with pleasure. At this point there seemed to be a cer- tain amount of "chucking out" going on at the back of the hall, and afterwards Dr. Rentoul was allowed to finish his remarks in comparative quietude. Mr. 'f. C. LONDON next moved a vote of confidence in the Government. This was seconded and carried. A TOW of thanks was also passed to the Chairman, on the motion of Major Pickmere, seconded by Alderman Harrison.

OVERFLOW MEETING. An "Overflow " meeting was held at the Conservative Club over which Alderman Francomb presided. Ad- dresses were given by the Chairman, Mr. A. Bennett, Councillor Cannel], Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, Councillor Heaton, Mr. R. Pierpoint, and Dr. RPntoul, and resolu- tions similar to those proposed at the other meeting were passed.

The expedition ag,ai nit the Lushais has had some more sharp fighting. Several towns have been captured and destroyed, and one of the freebooting rajahs is in the British camp as a prisoner.

AN EXTRAORDINARY MAP OF . . • RUNCORN. I . _ Now, ADVERTISING. At Runcorn County Court, on Saturday, before his Honour Judge Foulkes, the Borough and County Advertising Coinpilny, 2, Friar's-lane, 'Leicester, sought to recover .f,3 from Isaac Speakman, Bridge- street Ruworn, chemist, for an advertisement on a street map of Runcorn. Mr. Lake appeared for the plaintiffs and Mr. Burton was for the defendant. It was stated by Mr. Lake that in July last the plain- tiff's traveller attended at the defendant's shop,and produced a copy of a map of Runcorn, surrounded by different business advertisements. Mr. Speakman gave an order, and eicreed to pay £3. When the order was taken Mr. Speakman wished to have a pictorial as welt as a letterpress advertisement, and was told if he could get a photograph or b10...k of his business premises hi 4 wishes should receive attention. Not receiving this photograph after two applications the map was printed with the letter-press copy supplied, and was delivered on the 17th November: In March of this year the collec- tor applied for payment, and was met by the defendant saying the photograph had not appeared. Be offered £2 in payment of the claim, which was increased to £2 Zs. That sum was refused.—Mr. Burton, for the , defence, contended that the photograph was not inserted ! and that plaintiff's admitted the arrangement for it to be and he urged a denial that repeated applications I had been made for the negative.--His Honour pointed , out that the agreement signed was for the reservation of a certain space, without any stipulation whatever. In the faced a written contract like that produced, a ver- bal supplement to it could not be acknowledged. Ile must therefore give jndgment for the plaintiff. Another claim by the stime•firm against Wm. Lea and Sons, ironmongers, High-st., Runcorn' for £1 ss. was then heard. Mr. Lake again appeared for the plaintiffs- Ths evidence was in all reapects similar to the above, with one exception, namely, that Mr. Lea stated that he gave the order on condition that the map would be accurate and up to date. The sample shown was incor- rect, and defendant refused to pay. plaintiffs.—Mr. Timmins,'C.E., was called by defendant. He showed that the original Government survey was made in 1874, and had not been revised since. There were many streets not mentioned, and some of them were misnamed. A barber's saloon appeared as a bottling stores, and shops were on the wrong side of the streets, and several hundred yards away.—Mr. Lea: One place Is in my be& garden. (Laughter.)—His Honour stated that the prospectus intimated that the exact locality of each advertiser's business premises would be indicated on the Map. After what had been stated, it could hardly be staid that the map was" up to date." There were 10 or a dozen faults in it of an important nature, and the omission of the Alkali Works and the Ship Canal Works was serious. The map therefore could not be considered correct, and judgment must be given for the defendant.

J.- I had been in- her-company about twenty minutes, having met her on the Fair Ground. She said " Good night," and we parted it friendly fashion. At that time I had no suspicion that she was going to drown herself. She neither said nor did anything to lead me to that belief. She had told me that if anything hap- pened to her she dare not. go home. She wanted me to take her to Dublin, and I said I was not in the circum- stances to take her. I never saw her after I left her at the Finger-post. I heard on, Sunday she was drowned, and her father came and had a talk with me. The Coroner.—You spoke to her on the Wednesday night ?—Yes. Did you at that time lead her to believe that consider- inr, her position you would marry her P—l never led her to believe I would not marry her. Mrs. Lucy Greig was the next witness. She said de- ceased had told her she was in trouble, and dare not tell her parents. She said she should have to drown herself, and she dare not go home if her father found it out. She said she had written to Houghton twice while he was in Dublin, but had no answer, and when he returned he seemed as if he wanted to have nothing more to do with her. She said she would have to make a hole in the water. She had told Houghton her condi- tion, and he had said "If that be so it cannot be helped," and since then he had been cold and shunned her.

John Borchelt, of Victoria-st., and Sergeant Strong having given evidence of the finding of the body, The Coroner said the circumstances were quite clear. She was afraid Houghton would desert her, and the fear of her parents discovering her state led her to commit this act. The jury had only a legal duty to perform. The jury returned a verdict that the deceased com- mitted suicide while in a state of temporary insanity.

div.head: STRANGE DROWNING CASE AT ST. HELENS. DISAPPOINTMENT IN LOVE.
div.p: STRANGE DROWNING CASE AT ST. HELENS. DISAPPOINTMENT IN LOVE.

A somewhat singular drowning case was brought to light at St.Helens, on Sunday. Two men, whilst walking along the canal bank near the chemical works of Alderman M'Bryde, saw the body of a woman 'floating in the water. Information was given to the police, and the body was dragged to the side. The police ambulance was obtained,and the body conveyed to the mortuary in droundry-st., where gr.and Mrs. Cunningham, of 1, Endowment-row, off Traverse- it., St. Helens, subsequently identified it as that of their daughter Fanny; 11 years of age. The young woman left her home about eight o'clock on Saturday night, and with another girl visited the fairground at the end of Traverse-st. The companion left her a short time after- wards, and the deceased was then seen with a young man with whom she had been keeping, company for the last eight sr nine months. It has been ascertained that she +left him about a quarter-past eleven, and half an hotir later a woman named Bewshaw saw her alone in Barber-st. running in, the direction of the canal. She said to Mrs. Bewshaw, "Don't tell them anything if they come down here after me?' She went towards the canal, and Mrs. Bewshaw noticed her standing on the bank. Nothiag, further was heard of the matter until the body of the girl was found floating on Sunday. The father and mother of the deceased on Monday stated that for about eighteen months their daughter and •Joseph Houghton had kept company, and up to about Christmas had appeared to be on the most &flee- tionate terms. At the beginning of November last Houghton asked and obtained the consent of the father to the engagement,and furniture was purchased. Shortly after Christmas Messrs. Cannington and Shaves bottle, works, where Houghton was employed, went on short time and he obtained work in Dublin six weeks ago. While at Dublin Miss Cunningham wrote several times, but received no answer,and this appears to have affected her. He returned to St. Helens about a week aeo, but did not pay the usual visits to her house. The father. who worked at the Gerard's Bridge chemical yard, had to pass the bridge where his daughter's body was found at about five O'clock on Sunday morning, but did cot see her. When he learned that his daughter had not been home all night he went to see Houghton, who admitted lea.ving her at ten minutes past eleven on Saturday night: Mr_ Cunningham says Ow was always very timid, and would not even go to bed by herself. At times she had a hasty temper, but it would pass away in a few minsites. The young man Houghton stated that when he left her on Saturday night he had had no quarrel Ayith her, I and he noticed nothing in her manner which made him think that she was going to do anything to herself. The only way he could account for it was that she had asked him to take her back to Dublin with hire, and he refused. It appears that since leaving St. Helene, Houghton wandered about Yorkshire in search of work, hut could not get any, finallr going to Dublin. lie did not know that he was going to stay altogether at Dublin, and that was the reason ha did not wish to take her. Durine; her lover's absence in Dublin the poor girl frequently inquired from Mrs. Benyon (mother of Joseph .Benyon, who was also workin,, in Dublin) if she had sheard of him. She also candle7l to Mrs. Benyon her ,uondition, and her anxiety connected therewith. TEM INQUEST. _

He last saw her alive on Saturday morning, about half-past five. He saw her dead on Suni.ay, she having been taken out of the canal. She isevsn• threatened to take away her life, nor had ever done-anything to lead him to think she would do an. He was net aware of her condition.
