div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

On Thursday the remains of Fanny Cunningham, of Pkrr, St. Helens, who committed suicide by jumping into the!canal on Sunday last, were interred in the Catholic portion of St. Helens Cemetery. About 400 persons as- sembled at her late home in Endowment-row, including a large number of girls with whom she had worked at Messrs. Cannington and Shaw's bottle works. The coffin was covered with floral tributes from relatives, and friends, one made up in the form of an anchor being from her former workshop companions.

div.head: WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONARY ANNIVERSARY.
div.p: WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONARY ANNIVERSARY.

The anniversary in connection with the Wesleyan Foreign Missions was celebrated in the Wesleyan Chapel, Bold-st., on Sunday, by special sermons,de- livered by the Rev. Marshall Hartley, of London, general missionary secretary. There were large , congregations, that in the evening being especially I so, and the collections realised .612 us. 4d. On ' Monday evening the annual missionary meeting was held, Mr. Charles Parker presiding, and being supported on the platform by the Revs. Marshall Hartley, J. Gunnell, A. Freeman, T. Rosa, and J. Smith Spencer (late of South Africa), and Mr. w. Bennett. A hymn having been sung,prayer was offered up by the Rev. 'l'. Ross, after which the Rev. A. Freeman read the annual report. This showed that the total income raised front the circuit from the or- dinary sources,during the past year was £231. 18s. 21., an increase upon that of the previous year of £22 2s. 4d. : In addition to that various sums had been contributed for special objects. The Warrington branch of the cir- cuit had contributed £97 17s. 7d. an increase in the I year of £s3s. 51.—The chairman then addressed the , meeting. He said he sometimes thought that the very greatness of the foreign missionary society, the great area its operations covered, was a source ef weakness as well as of strength, that its influence became somewhat dissipated through the wideness of its area. He wished their influence could become more centralised and local- ised. He saw that at a district missionary meeting in Liverpool, at which a Warrington Wesleyan was the chairman, he said it was a question whether it was not letter to lavish their expenditure in fields that promised to be so fruitful rather than upon India. He (Mr. Parker) thought those who had an interest in a special phase of the work should be allowed to have their contributions devoted to that particular work. He should like to devote his to India, the brightest jewel in England's crown, that called most I upon them for missionary work. Our increasing con- nection with India and many other reasons called upon ' them to do all they could for India. Several years ago he tried through the Missionary House to get his prin- ciple of being allowed to contribute for special mission- ary objects, instead of to the general fund, adopted, but the idea was not favoured.—The Rev. J. Smith Spencer ' then delivered a lengthy speech. descriptive of the pro- gress of the missionary work in Pondoland. The history of that work, he said, had been one of profound disap- pointment ; and it had only been just lately that there had been anything like a break in the massive clouds that had rested upon the land, and any sort of introduc- tion to the incoming of a Christian day. There were only two European missionaries in Pondoland ; there were a few native missionaries and several evangelists, but oaly two mission stations. At present the Wesleyan ' Methodists were the only body that had missionaries there. The Roman Catholics had tried to get in. but when he left had not succeeded. The change that had sat in in Pondoland was singularly parallel to the change when Methodism cammenced in this country, and to , that which took place when Christianity began. la a kraal a long way from Christian people a young girl was I suddenly awakened to a sense of her sinfulness. She had never heard a preacher, but so plainly did she hear a voice speaking to her heart as if from heaven that she I left her friends and relatives and walked a considerable cdstance to the nearest Christian kraal and told what she had heard and felt, renouncing heathenism, and sin- bracing Christianity. Other similar cases were des- cribed by tlo speaker. It seemed, he remarked, as if Christianity was in the air, and then he related how a marvellous revival took Oace, the natives rushing down to ihe river to be baptised ; and have the fat, and red ochre with which they smeared their bodies washed off Iby each other. The red paint stained the water for some distance and the natives along the banks supposed there was a trihal fight, and that the stain was blood, until they discovered the cause. Women , who went to draw water for the evening meal found it too defiled to drink, and their kusbands rushed out with ! assegais and threats to destroy the defiler of the water, :being pacified with difficulty on reaching the baptismal scene. The extraordinary and sadden conversion of a bloodthirsty witch doctress when happening to enter a service of the new Christians in abut was detailed. The dangers to which missionaries, and the persecution to Wiliell the converts were exposed in Fondoland were also deseribed.—The Rev. M. Hartley then spoke. He gavel seine details tv. to the finances of the society. He men- , tioned that the ordinary home income was in 1891 £l3BO ' above that of the previous year, and was £127,000, from all sources, but the expenditure was £129,000. Methodism had had an increase of 600 last year, one for I every 6,30 Methodists and abroad it had increased by 1 hi ' 23. The raanagetnent of the society he said airily cost 5 per cent.—l vote of thanks, was accorded to the deputation and the Chairman, and a motion was passed appointing the usual committee, Mr. W. Barlow trea- surer. the Rev. A. Freeman and Mr. R. Smith secretar- ies.—The collection during the evening realised £l7 es, 60.
WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY. CLOSING CONCERT OF THE SEASON.

The fourth and concluding concert for the season was given by the above-named society In the Public Mall, on Tuesday evening. There was a large attendance. The composition which formed the subject of the principalperformance on this occasion was the cantata "The ancient mariner," by Mr. F. J. Barnett, this being succeeded by a. miscell- aneous concert. The band and chorus numbered two hundred performers, Mr. Frank H. Crossley con- ducting with hie accustomed ability, and the prin- cipal vocalists being Madame Conway, soprano, Miss Hilda Wilson, contralto, Mr. James Leyland, tenor, and Mr. A. S. Kinnell, bass. The concert was on the whcle exceedingly successful, the audience being worked up to a high pitch of enthusiasm in several instances during the rendering of the cantata. This was especially the ease when Madame Conway and Miss Hilda Wilson joined in the duet " But tell me, tell me, speak again," which was beautifully executed. The recitative and air" And now this spell was snapt,' sung by Mr. A. S. Kinnell was a very fine performance on his part, while the accompainments to this passage ' were played with splendid effect. The choruses were, throughout well given. The second part of the pro- gramme began with an intermezzo by the orchestra and organ, from " Cavalleria Rusticana," by Kascagne, which was executedin a masterly style, Then came Miss Hilda Wilson with the song "Voices of the angels," which was so charmingly given that the audience accorded her a vociferous encore; and she repeated part of the song. Madame Conway received an enthusiastic recall for her bril- liant execution of "The songs the children sang," and the audience were by no means caused to repent their encore by her piquant rendering of "Twickenham Ferry" with which, in compliance, she favoured them. Mr. A. S. ffinnell was warmly recalled for his "I'm a roamer," and repeated the latter portion; and Miss Wil- son for Meyerbeer's song "Noble signors," from "Les Hugenot's," was similarly and deservedly honoured. Mr. James Leyland sang "The island of dreams" by Stephen Adams; and the concert was concluded with Gounod's chorus "By Babylon's wave," which from the manner in which it was rendered gave a very satisfac- tory finish to a most successful entertainment. We may mention that the organ in the Public Hall was used on Tuesday night for the last time by the Musical Society as it will shortly be removed from the Hall prior to the conversion of the building into a theatre. The Society have, however, seamed four more date for concerts for the next season from the Public Hall Co., but these con- certs will probably be held in the theatre, after which the Society will have to find other accomodation. •

div.head: PROPOSED NEW PUBLIC HALL FOR WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE PROPOSED NEW PUBLIC HALL FOR WARRINGTON.

On Tuesday afternoon a meeting was held in the ante-room of the Public Hall for the purpose of considering the question of providing another Public Hall in Warrington, the present Public Hall Company being about to wind up, and the hall sold for the purposes of a permanent theatre. The Mayor (Alderman Greenall) presided, and there were also present Messrs. John Ryland' s John White, Henry Greenall, L. W. Rylands, Robert Garnett, Wm. Johnson, W. E. Atkin, and F. H. Crossley. The MAYOR said that plans were about to be submit- ted to the Town Council as to the desirabilitiy of cen- tralizing all the municipal offices at the Town Hall, and the police station was included in the scheme. With regard to the proposal to erect a new Public Hall, he did not think it was at all likely that the matter would be considered by the Council. Mr. RYLANDS said the present hall was built because it was felt at the time that there was a necessity for it ; it was not built with the object of making a profit. That was a secondary consideration, and during the 30 years the hall had been in existence it would be admit- ted it had been a great advantage to the town. There , was no question now that it had become too small for existing requirements. He theught it would be admit- ted that there was a necessity for a Public Hall for War- rington, and the ratepayers would feel all the more interested in it if the matter was taken up by the Cor- peration. He suggested that a deputation be appointed to wait upon the General Purposes Committee. Mr. JOHN WHITE said that if the Corporation would consent to take the matter up, it would be the best way out of the difficulty. This was a matter that could not very well wait. The Public Hall had been sold, and for all practical purposes, it would not be available for public meetings next winter, with the exception of three or four, for which it had been reserved. For all prac- tical purposes the room would be no longer available for public meetings, and it was therefore desirable that they should come to a settlement at the earliest passible moment. Only five minutes had elapsed since the final deed was done by which the building had been conveyed to the people who had bought it. Therefore he felt that not a moment ought to be Lost, and that the Corpora- tion should be approached at once. There were two dificulties to be faced. People would say that they had made away with the Public Hall. But that was no 'business of the public, as the hall belonged to a com- pany, and the directors were only responsible to the shareholders. He had been connected with the hall since its erection, and they had always endeavoured,not only to make it a convenience for the public, but a pay- ing concern for the shareholders. In these respects they had succeeded very well, because the dividend had never been less than 3i per cent., and it had occasionally been as high as 5 per cent. He considered that that was a very satisfactory record. (Hear, hear.) People would say that years ago they could not make the Public Hall pay without theatrical performances. How was it to be made to pay in the future ? For a few years there would be a difficulty in making a new Public Hall pay, but now the population was nearly double what it was when the building was put up. He moved, "That a committee Le at once appointed to approach the Corporation, and to take such steps as they may think necessary for the erection of a new Public Ball." Mr. ROBERT GARNETT, in seconding the motion,said he shnuld like to know the probable cost of the new build- ng. Be did not think it was for a number of gentlemen like themselves, with others added to them, to go out of their way to benefit the people of Warrington. It would be better for the Town Council to take the matter up. Other Corporations did so, and he did not see why the Warrington Corporation should not build a hall. Mr. JOHN WHIT' said he calculated that a new Hall would cost £5,000. The resolution having been passed, it was decidedjthat the following gentlemen should be appointed to wait upon the General Purposes Committee on Monday, May 9th :—Messrs. John Itylands, Robert Garnett, J. C. Parr, L. W. Reynolds, John White, T. Glazebrook Rylands, James Marson, and John Dun. Mr. Rupert Crossley was appointed secretary pre tom.

Fire broke out early on Monday morning in the store, depot of the London General Omnibus Company, Pad- dington-green, and the entire building and contents were destroyed. The loss is covered by insurance. At a meeting held at IVestrninster,on Wednesdav night, under the presidency of the Duke of Norfolk it was resolved to found in London a refuge for the homeless poor as a memorial of the lata Cardinal Manning.
" WEBSTER'S RANDLE."
A KARIKTER SKETCH.

• "Ord Webster's Randle " wur a mou------ Aw never con forge; ; His cuaint, quare an' forrin' yarns Are buzzin' tue yet! He's made nae dabble up an' skrike, Ez if my ribs war crack'd ; • Or if aw'd bin a sheuf o' corn, An' wi' a swippo wack'd ! The tales he used to tell surnames— An' he'd a lot r store— Wad cause a sidesman t' smile i'ehureil, An' mek a Parson roar !

He's bin o'er every yard o' th' globe, Fro China to Chowbent ; An' mostly made hissel a-worn, So wheere the dule he went. No chap wur better known then him, I' Boston or Belle Vue, An' mony a time his ship's bin rack'd- 'Twixt Bradford an' Peru! He allus wur a welcome guest At ev'ry Forrin' Coort ; It mattert nowt, when "Randle" coons, They'd allus lots o' spoort. The Emperor o' China's axt Him mony a time to sup On fav'rite dishes—cowd brids' masts, Rot pie, an' roasted pup! He's dined i' Egypt wi' th' Khedive, On peyse an' curried duck; An made a meyl o' bread an' cheese ' At th' "Owls Neest " Black-bruck He's drove a engine i' Japan, Cut turf i' Coleraine, Drunk vodki i' Sent Petersburg, An' revits made i' Spain ! Once, wen he went to Timbuctoo, Wen Bashaw wur a " kid,"
lie sent sum Checky-Micks-LCain'a breed— An' a bonny Sammy Brid. ' WM: A Wayter Fluzzert coom ez weel, No thicker then a twig; 14-44a4r: That favvert nothin' haul 80 mitch
Ez a sarpent or a snig ! • I' music, too, he wur no foo, • • • On Orgins or Trambones ; We'n heerd him bring eawt fro one note, • Four different semitones! B flat, B sharp, B.natural,

, An' B—well, here aw'm lost ; But it wur summut made us roar, An' very nearly host 1 In short, his aiquil is'nt wick, Per deawnreet fun an' glee : So wen he cums abeawt eawr place, May aw be theer to see ! An' wen he's done, an' "hops his twig," An' King Death stops his beer, May he ne'er find a hotter shop Than he's bin used to here ! TUM 0' PEGS ! Nyowton God bless o'. April 29th, 1892.

div.head: PUBLICANS AND POLICEMEN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: PUBLICANS AND POLICEMEN AT RUNCORN.

Before Mr. John Brundrit and Dr. Steele. at Run- corn Petty Se,sionii, on Monday, Charles Thomas Bridgeman,landlord of the beerhouse Bird in Hand, Halton-road, was summoned on two informations charging him with having on the Bth April, sup- plied intoxicating liquor to two constables—Charles Dutton, and George Dickenson—while on duty and without the permission of their superior officer.— Mr. A. Fletcher, of Northwich, prosecuted, and stated that about four o'clock on the date named, P.C. Di6censon aud an officer in plain clothes en- tered the defendants house and were supplied. Dicken- son was not off duty but would have been in the course of a few minutes. Dutton who came in while the other officers were there, had, however, only just entered up- on his duties, and although he was only in the house five minutes, he was supplied with two pints of beer. and then went on his best. The result was, that about seven o'clock he was drunk. The prosecution did not say that he had got all the drink at the defendant's house but it must have had a considerable effect upon him. The question was never put to the officer as to whether or not they were on duty. Mr. Fletcher pointed out that the penalty for a first offence was £lO and for a second offence £2O, and said they knew what comments had been made with reference to publicans and the police in Runcorn, and it might have boen thought that 1 *very one would have taken warning. Tho authorities considered the offence a very serious one and pressed for • heavy penalty. Defendant had not kept the house very long, the license being transferred to him on tie Bth February.—Tho defendant pleaded guilty and said he did not think he was infringing the law. One officer told I him he was off duty, and as the other was dressed in I exactly similar manner, he thought that he also was off duty. He had had no nistics with respect to serving officers or otherwise. He was ignorant of the law.— Superintendent Atherton said the defendant came to the house with a good character.—Mr. Brundrit said defend- ant ought to have known the law on such a matter or else not have had the license. It was a serious matter that publicans sheuid supply policemen with drink 1 whilst on duty, and a fine of 40s. and costs would be I imposed in each case, total £4 17s.

div.head: ST. PAUL'S SALE OF WORK.
div.p: ST. PAUL'S SALE OF WORK.

The annual sale of work in connection with St. Paul's Church, Warrington, was held in the Infants School, on Monday afternoon. There was a large attendance. Amongst those present being the Vicar (The Rev. 11. V. Pigot) and Mrs. Pigot, the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Greenall) the Rev. J. C Pigot (St. Belem) and Mrs. Pigot, Mrs. Bell (Appleby'„ Mrs. Irving, Mr. and Mrs. Birley (Lytham), Alias Pigot, Mrs. Arthur Pigot,Mr. Herbert Pigot, the Rev. T. M. R. Ycung-liughes, the Rev. F. Shirtcliffe, Mrs. Beamont, Mrs. John White, Mrs. Lyon, MS. Robert Davies, Mrs. Willis, Mrs. D. Jones, Mrs. Wilkinson (Timperley), Dr. White, and Messrs. Robert Davies, D. W. Piuney,D. , Jones, Thomas Morris, James Smethurst, William Richardson, Joseph Lawless, and Chorley. In a circular which has been issued by the Vicar, it is stated "That the needs of the parish increase each year, and some most important objects are entirely dependent on the proceeds of the anneal sale. The first charge is to provide the mission lady's salary. The value of her services is highly appreciated,and it is recognised by all, that this item of expenditure brings in an excellent re- turn for the outlay. It is also neisessary to devote solve of the profits of Vie sale to the mission fund, for provid- ing books and Sunday School prizes at AR Saints', Bewsey, to pay for gas, to., in Heath-side echoels for evening classes and meetings on week days, and to nate a contribution towards the St. Paul's Sunday school fund. Besides these objects, whieh have always received support from the sale, it will be necessary in future to look for some help towards the curate fund. The necessity for this arises from the withdrawal of the suliscrintions of some of those who have helped the parish in past years." The stalls as usual were well filled with An assortment of useful and fancy goods. Mrs. John Chorltev, Mrs. Gibson Smith, Mrs. Peacock°, Miss White, and Miss Lily Mackie were in charge of No. 1 Stall. No. 2 stall was under the care of Mrs. Geddes, Mrs. Depherd, Mrs. W. J. Burgess (Liverpool), and No. 3 under the ears of Mrs. Thomas Morris,Mrs. John Hesketh,Miss Coubreugh, and Miss Burton. The other stalls were under the direction of the following ladies :—No. 4, Mrs. Finney and Miss Finney ; No. 5, Mrs. Smethurst, Mrs. William Richard- son, Mrs. J. Richardson, Miss Smethurst, and Miss Reid; No. 8, Miss Craik and Miss Atherton ; No. 7, refreshment stall, Mrs. Highley, Mrs. Pryer. Mrs. Joseph Lawless, Miss Westwell, Miss Braide, and Miss Shawcmss ; No. 8, flower Pahl Miss Griffiths, Miss A. Smethurst; bran pie. Miss W. Griffiths. The MAYORESS who opened the sale a work said she understood the speeches were to be short, and, there- fore, one would not be expected from her. They all understood the object of the sale of work, and how much depended Upon it in the parish. She asked those present to assist in the object in view, and hoped that before the evening was over the stalls would be emptied of their contents. She had much pleasure in declaring the sale open, (Applause.) •,1 4.1 Ms or s had set a Mr. Romewr DAMS said the y es most commendable example of brevity in the excetient speech she hail just delivered. He was sorry to say that he had been made a Victim already- He had not got to the end of the room when, of all things, a grindstone was offered to him. Be did not want one, its he had several about his premises a.ready, but he was vicuna. ized to the extent of purchasing it. (Latrghter.) He hoped others would follow his exatnple. They all knew why money was round, namely, that it might roll away from theta the easier. (Hear, hear.) Councillor SMETHURST moved and Mr. T. MORRIS seconded, a hearty vote of thanks to the mayor and Mayoress for their presence, to the latter for opening the sale of work and the MAJOBESS briefly returned thanks. During the afternoon and evening concerts were given at intervals by the members of the choir, and Messrs. Muratti, Sons and Co., Limited, had forwarded& quantity of ciearettes for the smoking,. concert=. Tea was also provided. The sale of work realized £164 14s, 9d.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY OUTRAGE AT LATCHFORD.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY OUTRAGE AT LATCHFORD.
--- - - - -- AATG}IMAN - LIRDE4tOUSLT ATTA CK ED.

SUPPOSED ATTEMPT TO FIRE THE STATION. ' An attempt was made early on Sunday morning to set Ere it is supposed, to the new, and almost completed, railway station, at Latchford,erected by the Ship Canal Company on the deviation line. A night watchman left the station at half-past five o'clock on Sunday morning, his place being taken by a man named Abraham Thowas, who is about 60 years of age,and who lives at No. 23,Sand- hill-terrace, Wash-lane, Latchford. There seems to have been no apprehension of danger, as the night watchman went home, and Thomas was left alone in charge of the premises. When his daughter arrived, at about twenty minutes past eight, with his breakfast, she was horrified to discover her father lying on his back on the ground in an unconscious condition,bleedwg pro- fusely from a severe wound on the head. Blood was also issuing from his nose and mouth. As soon as she reccvered from the shock which the unexpec'ed sight had produced, she obtained the assistance of a man named Richard Baker, a "walking ganger" employed on the Ship Canal, and with his and other assistance the unconscious watchman was carried to his home in Wash- lane, and attended by the doctor from the Ship Canal Hospital at Latchford. Several hours afterwards Ttiobnas recovered consciousness, and when interrogated as to the events of the early morning, he was understood to gay that, hearing a man walking about the premises, he went up to him. He struck him with his stick, and a struggle took place between the men. While it was pro- ceeding he was assailed from behind by a blow on his head, which rendered him unconscious. He remembered nothing more till he awoke about dinner-time, and found himself at home.

--rolice-Constable Bell was the officer on duty in the neighbourhood at the time, and certain inquiries have been instituted by him, I). S. Monaghan and others, from which it appears that small bundles of shavings and wood had been disposed in six different parts of the station, and it is thought that it was the intention of several men to set fire to them with the object of burn- ing down the station in revenge for their dismissal from the service of the company. Shavings and wood were placed in each subway, as well as in four different parts of the platform. Blood was to be seen on Monday morn- ing in the gentlemen's lavatory, where it is believed the struggle took place, and where the watchman was knocked dcwn, He was then dragged into the porter's room, as his head was found on the doorstep and his body on the door of the room. An unsuccessful attempt had been made to ignite several of the pieces of wood, and it was the sound of men moving about that drew Thomas's attention to what was gning on. However, the men evidently took alarm at the course of events, as they went away, no damage having been done to the station, which is, in future, to be more carefully guarded by the addition of a second watchman The injured man is progressing favourably, and is now said to be out of danger, though he is still confined to his bed, and is in a very weak state. The affair has created, as May be imagined,- consider- able excitement throughout Latchford. It is, somewhat remarkable that, if the men intended to fire the station, 1 they should have waited until daylight, when they had much less chance of success in their nefarious operations. We learn that the Ship Canal Co., have offered a reward of £2O for the discovery of the perpetraters of the mysterious outrage ; and it is earnestl: to be hoped that the endeavours to discover them will be crowned with success.

div.head: DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT ELLESMERE PORT. ARREST ON SUSPICION.
div.p: DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT ELLESMERE PORT. ARREST ON SUSPICION.

It is feared that the disastrous fire on the Ship Canal at Ellesmere Port on Monday, by which an engine shed, two cement stores, a testing shed, and two dwelling huts were totally destroyed, together with 3,000 bags, four railway trucks, and 4,70 tons of cement, was the work of some mischievous boys. Police-constable Finchett, Ellesmere Port, who has investigated the origin of the fire, had his attention drawn to the movements of three boys. They were interrogated, with the result that one, named Young, aged thirteen, has been taken into custody on a charge of setting fire to the Ship Canal Company's property, and will be brought up to-day (Saturday), The total damage is estimated at £1,500. Five patients in the Ship Canal Hospital had to be hurriedly removed, but fortunately the fire did not extend to that structure

div.head: EXECUTION OF Mc BRIGHTON MURDEREIL
div.p: EXECUTION OF Mc BRIGHTON MURDEREIL

George Henry Wood, 29, railway porter, was hanged in Lewes Goal on Tuesday, for the murder at Brighton, in December last, of Edith Jeal, five years of age, who was found violated and strangled in a shed. In the procession to the scaffold,Wood, who looked exceedingly pale, walked with great firmness. Billington quickly placed the rope round his heck, and whilst the minister was reading the sentence "In the midst of life we are in death," the bolt was drawn, and Wood disappeared int* the pit. The execution was carried out in an exceed- ingly prompt manner.

On Monday morning, about nine o'clock, a sea- man named Henry Fisher, met with a shocking death while fulfilling his duties on board the schooner Rescue, of Poole, Captain Townsley. As usual with vessels bound for Runcorn, the Rescue had been moored in the Sloyne, near Rock Ferry, and the anchor had been raised in readiness for being towed up the river by the Shia Canal Com— pany's steamer Dagmar. It was found that the anchor was "foal," and Fisher went over the bow to set it right. A THEATRE BURNED DOWN IN AMERICA.. LOSS OF LIFE AND MANY PERSONS INJURED. r PHILADELPHIA. THI7II9DAT.—A terrible fire broke out in the grand Central Theatre here on Wednesday night, where a spectacular play was being performed involving the use of much inflammable scenery. • The auditorium was fortunately only partially filled with people, but as soon as the flames were perceived, a rush was made for the door. The weaker ones were borne down by the press behind, and the crushing, fighting, and struggl- ing were awful to witness. One, maddened by desire to get free, actually drew a pocket knife and cleared' tway through the crowd by cutting down those' who obstructed him. Several persons were treated at the hospital for wounds thus inflicted. Fully 70 men and boys were injured in the theatro,rnany seriously. Most of them aresuffering from burns on the face. The patients are all being treated in hospital. It is reported that two men and four women connected with the company which was performing at the theatre are missing. Their friends are unable to And them, and it is feared they have Inns their lives. PIII LADELPHIA, THURSDAY (LATSR).—AII efforts to Gls- cover the whereabouts of missing members of the thea- trical company have failed, and it is now considered al- most certain that they are buried in the runis thst building. It is also feared that the burns received by five boys and two men among the injured now in hospi- tal, will prove fatal.

CONSIIARING that 1104:att Rule has Ulster been again and again declared and the, Unionists, to be dead, it must be remarked 1 that for, a corpse it has shown itself very lively of late. The fact. is the Tories and Liberal Unionists cannot leave it alone; they hover about it as moths hover about a flame; and, .as is the casewith. moths, there is every likelihood as to some of them that it will result in their extinction. The Dzura of DEVON- SHIRE devoted nearly the wholeof the long speech I which he made at I)erby, on Monday evening, to the question of Home Rule;, but it was a dreary performance, for it was unrelieved either by any new idea on the subject, or any new expression of an old,idea. Still, As he is-the elaief of a party,it is due to his position that attention should,, be given..to what he has to. say—particularly as. he had previously been silent for some time. Speak- ing of Sir WILLIAM HARnousa as an Opportanist, the Duke of Devonshire said:.—

The first thing which an Opportunist pclitican bast° do is to calculate correctly the forces with which he has to deal—(hear, hear)—andjf it is found that he has miscalculated the strength of those forces, if the cause which he has deserted as a hopeless one should prove to be not only the right but the suncessful. cause—(hear, hear),—if. the in- stitution which he abandons survives in spite of his defection ana notwithstanding his attacks,then he is convicted of what must be in the eyes of ,Opportunist statesmen worse than a crinse,, and he has perpetrated a blunder.

- - We don't see how this can be mad e: to apply to the member for Derby; but, if tha word " move- ment" be substituted-for "institution,' the cap, is one which may basaid to fit to. perfection the head of the Liberal Unionists. There was a time when he and his friends spoke of themselves as the real Liberal party, and when, to do them jug- tice,they believed that the forces, they commanded were sufficient to overwhelm the movement,for Home Rule. Rut how do they. stand now, after aix years. of agitation? They are the mere rem- nant of a remnant; so small as to number and in- fluence that the Tories ask, at every bye-election, where their votes are to be found, and, much to 'their annoyance, they can get no satisfactory answer. It, is the Liberal Unionists who have so strangely miscalculated. their strength, which, never really great, is a daily diminishing quantity. Reference was made to the meetings, which have been held by the Ulster party, and to. the resolu- tions of protest which they have passed. On a similar occasion, a few years ago, Lord RANDOLPH Cuuscurra, said—" Ulster will fight and Ulster will be right ;" but his lordship has probably by this changed his mind; and the Duke of DavoNsuraz certainly has no sympathy with threatenings or slaughter, Speaking of the Ulster resolve "to take no part in the elections or proceedings of such a Parliament, of which, if ever constituted, we shall be forced to rep udiate the authority," he

Later on he ad- ministered another cold douche by speaking of "those miserable sortarian and religious feuds and animosities ; " but went on to affirm that it was the power of the British Parliament which had hitherto preserved the peace between " these hostile creeds." Still, it must be admitted that the peace has often been broken—and broken too by the men who have been in the ascendant, id- though they have been and are yet in a minority. Cymro, A Tradesman, and A Working-man.— Next week.

The Anarchists have shown themselves so active of late that there is an uneasy feeling, especially on the Continent, as to what may be the result of the May Day labour celebrations. At Colchester, the Trades and Labour Council are to have. a demonstrationi which will be followed by a special service in the Church. This is a good sign; it s better than denunciation, or attempted suppres- sion.

-- The inquest at St. Helens, on Wednesday, on the body of the girl Palmy Cunningham reveals a lad story of seduction and suicide. The indiffer- ence of her lover, under critical circumstances, !teems to have driven the poor girl out of her mind; • hence the verdict of "suicide whilst in a state of taraporary insanity." KICKING CASH AT WIDNES.

Before Mr. F. B. at Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, Thos. Griffin and Jas. Melvin, of Warrington- road aid Peter Ryland of Midwood-street, were charged with wounding Daniel Gilmore, of Midwood-street, with Intent to do him grievous bodily harm. Evidence was given showing that the prisoner had severely kicked the injured man whom, Dr. O'Keeffe stated, was unable to appear. The prisoners were remanded until Monday. At a meeting of the Runcorn Lifeboat Crewe Division of the Sons of Temperance, on Saturday evening the presidency of Mr. Thomas Clarke, the members had under consideration the Bill for prohibiting the sale of intoxicating liquors to children, down for the second reading the House of Commons on May 11th. The mea- sure, which has been introduced by Mr. Conybeare, sets forth " that every holder of a license, whe sells, or delivers, or allows any persons to sell any description of intoxicating liquor, to any person apparently under the age of 16 years, shall be liable to a penalty of not exceed ing 20s. for the first offence, and not exceeding 40s. for a seco id and any subsequent offence." The subject was discussed, and it was unanimously resolved, on the motion of Mr. Thomas Cooke, seconded by Mr. J. Jones, to send a petition to the House of Commons in support of the Bill, the same to be signed by the Chairman and the co-secretaries, Messrs. Thomas Cooke and Edward Key. It was also resolved to request Mr. J. T. Brunner M.P., to present the petition.

THE WIDNES WOUNDING CASE.

Francis Gaynor, of Ellison-st., was again brought before the Widnes magistrates on Thursday, charged with unlawfully wounding his wife, Mary Ann, by kick- ing her on the 2nd inst.—Dr. Hudson said the condition of the woman had improved, and she would probably be able to appear in a week. The prisoner was remanded for that period. FALL FROM A. SCAFFOLD AT RUNCORN. While assisting in discharging a vessel at Runcorn Docks on Tuesday, Thomas Outram, of Canal-street, was knocked off a scaffold by a tub swinging at the end of a crane and his thigh was fractured. P.C. Crowder seeing the injured man being conveyed home in a barrow bandaged up the li m b and had him carried on a stretcher, thus considerably easing his pain.

Oh Monday evening a public meeting was hold in the new Mission Room, West Batik, Widnes, for the purpose of inaugurating a branch of the Church Army Brigade in connection with the parish of Widnes. The vicar (Rev. G. H. Garrett) presided, and the Rev. C. Musgrave Brown, M.A., delivered an address. Captain Goater, who is to have charge of the work, also spoke,and made an urgent appeal for workers to assist in the new under- taking.
WIDNES FREE LIBRARY.

At the annual Meeting-o-f—t-h-i-;-C-o-in-Mittee on Wedne s day, Mr. Midwood presiding, Mr. H. Wade Deacon was unanimously re-elected Chairman. The report of the Librarian showed that the reading room had been open 27 days in April and the total attendance had been 14,252, against 11,527 in March. The total number of books consulted was 5,418, being an increase of 1,149 in the lending department and a decrease of 35 in the reference department compared with corresponding month last year. The boys room had been well attended and had proved a great boon on the adult readers.

Mary O'Donnell, wife of Patrick O'Donnell, of Back Mersey-st., attempted to commit suicide on Thursday morning by cutting her throat with a razor. She was found by her husband at ten o'clock lying on the kitchen floor in a pool of blood, and Inspector Cooper and P.C. Crowder, hearing of the occurrence, went to the place and stopped the bleeding of the wound. Afterwards Dr. McDougall attended the injured woman and ordered her removal to the Workhouse Hospital, where she was subse- quently conveyed. It appears that the woman had been suffering from depression for some time past, and her mental burden was increased on Saturday, when her husband was thrown out of work. TABLBAUX VIVANT'S AT RUNCORN.

In aid of the fund for the completion of St. Michael's chancel, a series of tableaux vivants were represented in Shaw-st. School, on Thursday evening, by the follow- ing ladies and gentlemen :—Mrs. Jesse Timmins, Mrs.N. R. Martin, Miss Timmins, Miss Lightburn, Messrs. N R. Martin, H. C. Beeley, and Rev. G. 11. Seeley. While many of the tableaux were highly artistic and dramatic, others a p pealed t) the humourous faculty, and the large audience that assembled thoroughly enjayed the enter- tainment. Each representation was accompanied by music appropriate to the scene depicted, Miss E. Crosby ably officiating at the piano. At intervals songs were given by Miss Stubbs and Miss Lightburn and Masters Timmins save selections on the violin aad piano. div.head: STREET OBSTRUCTION BT NAVVIES AT RUNCORN.
div.p: STREET OBSTRUCTION BT NAVVIES AT RUNCORN.

Before Mr. Jas. Handley at Runcorn Police Court,on Tuesday, Thos. Kelly, a navvy, was charged with ob- structing High-st., by loitering thereon and refusing to move when requested to do so by Inspector Cooper.— P.C. Crowder said on the previous night about 14 Irish- , men were blocking the footpath near the Post Office. Some of them moved at once, but when he had left them they returned to the footpath and " boo'd "at him iu degance. He went back and spoke to them quietly, and the prisoner went on the footpath while he was standing there, and Inspector Cooper instructed him to lock the man up.—lnspector Cooper described the hoot- ing and shouting that took place, and said that for the last few weeks they had been troubled by gangs of men obstructing footpaths, and it did not matter who was coming along, they would not move. It was no use one policeman speaking to them, and this case was brought as an example. A fine of Is., and costs 7s. was imposed. UMBRELLAS RRCOVERED.—J. and W. DUrrON, Sankepet., Warrington.— Advt.

MARRIAGE OF MISS N. HANDLEY OF RUNCORN. A large audience assembled in Bethesda Congrega- tional Church on Thursday morning to witness the nuptials of Miss N. Handley, second daughter of Mr. W. Handley, of Runcorn, to Mr. A. G. calvert of York. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. S. B. Ilandlev, of Birmingham, (uncle of the bride) assisted by the Rev. John Simpson, the pastor. The bride who was given away by her father was attired in a blue costume, trimmed with cream silk, with a cream hat and she carried a beautiful bouquet of white flowers. She was attended by her sister, Miss Linnie Handley as brides- maid, who wore green cloth dress,trimmed with silk and a Tuscan hat, with white velvet and lilies of the valley. Her throat was adorned with a gold crescent and pearl brooch, the gift of the bridegroom. In her hand she carried a posy of daffodils. After the usual formalities had been gone through, the happy couple received the congratulations of numerous friends, and the wedding party had breakfast at the residence of Mr. Handley Later in the day Mr. and Mrs. Calvert departed to Betwys Coed, where the honeymoon will be spent. Many numerous and valuable presents had been received.

MARRIAGE OF MISS L. WAREING, OF WIDNES.

The ancient church of St. Luke's, liarnworth, was the scene of a most interesting marriage on Saturday after- noon, and the sacred edifice was crowded with those anxious to witness the ceremony. The contracting parties were Lilian, third daughter of Major Wareinv,of Mill Brow, Widnes, a member of Prescot Board of Guardians and of Widnes School Board, and Ffenry,third on of Mr. David Auer, of Buda Pastb, kustria. The officiating clergymen were the Revs. G. A. Le Bert (vicar of St. Ambrose), and J. R. Jones (curate in charge of St. Luke's.) The bride, who was given away by her father, was attired in a brown cloth dress, with hat to match, trimmed with ostrich feathers, and she carried in her hand a bouget of pink roses. She was attended by her sisters,Miss Wareing ana Miss Ma bel Wareing,who wore costumes of grey cloth, fastened at the throat with swallow brooches, set with pearls, the gift of the bride- groom. Mr. Martin J. Hammill, of St. Helens, was best man, the other groomsman being Mr. J. Miniata,of Man- chester. After the ceremony and the usual formularies had been gone through, the wedding party were driven to Mill Brow,whence the newly married couple departed amid showers of rice for London, en route to the conti- nent,where the honeymoon is to be spent. The presents were very numerous and valuable. In the evening Major and Mrs. War3ing gave a reception, at which were present many friends.

FRODSHAM PRIMROSE LEIGOE.

The annual meeting of members was held in the Town Hall, on Wedaesday evening, under the presidency of Mr. James Reynolds, R.C. There was a good attend- ance. Mr. A. Thomas (hon. treasurer) submitted the financial statement, from which it appeared that there was a balance in hand of £33 10s. 9d. The statement was approved. Colonel Ashton gave the warden's re- port. It set forth that on the 19th inst. the habitation contained 19 knights 19 dames, and 731 associates, total, 769, against 703 last year. The members residing in the various districts wero—Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship 661, against 631 a year ago ; Helsby 72, against 44, and Alvanley 36, against 28. The election of officers was then proceeded with. Mr. James Reynolds was re-appointed Ruling Councillor, and Mr. Thomas treasurer. It was announced that through ill-health Mrs. Ashton was forced to relinquish the office of secre- tary. A high compliment was paid to her for the valu- able services rendered by her since the formation of the habitation. Their success was the result of her arduous effort. It was decided to leave the appointment in the hands of the Executive Committee. Colonel Ashton was re-chosen warden. The following were appointed as the Executive Committee : Mrs. James Reynolds, Mrs. Weaver, Mrs. Thomas, Mr. H. Reynolds, Mrs. Steele, Mrs. Murray, Mrs. Barff, Mrs. White, Mrs. G. Garrett, Mrs. Collinson, Miss Wright, Miss E. P. Wright, Miss Laycock, Miss Davies, Messrs. R. Watson, H. Lowe, Broady, and S. Davies. On the motion of the Chair- man, seconded by Dr. Weaver, a vote of confidence in the Government was passed, and Mr. R. Lewis, of Widnes, delivered an address on politics. Selections of music were given during the evening.

DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. PROPOSED SUNDAY SCHOOL DEMONSTRATION AT WIDNES. On Tuesday evening a meeting of delegates from the various Sunday Schools in Widnes was held in Lacey-street School for the purpose of considering the advisability of holding all the Sunday School treats at the same time and arranging a" walking day," similar to those of Runcorn and Warrington. There were about twenty delegates present, and Mr. S. Drought was voted to the chair. After a long discussion the meeting decided that it was not possible to hold the treats and demonstration on the same day this year, but it was resolved to have & demonstration on the afternoon of Saturday, July 2nd, and it is hoped that every School in the town will join in and make the display of the power of Sunday Schools as successful as possible. it is proposed to defray the expense of the demon- stration by public subscription.

GARLAND, Ironmonger, Bridge-st., Warrington. THE ENGLISH DRAUGHTS CHAMPIONSHIP.

The tournament for the English draughts cham- pionship, which commenced at the Polytechnic on Easter Monday, was brought to a conclusion on Tuesday evening last, by Jordan, of London, defeat- ing Richmond, of Marsden, in the final heat, and thus securing the championship and the first prize of £25 and a gold medal. Richmond takes second prize, £lO, Keor of Bristol, third, .£5 ; whilst the 4th and sth arizes (.£5) were divided by Tescheleit (the London champion) and Dunne, of Warrington. Our local champion made a good score against Richmond the runner up, viz., won 1, lost 2, and 5 games drawn. He was unfortunate in being drawn against Richmond in the second round, or would most likely have secured one of the three major prizes. The new champion is a young man only 20 years of age.

Mn. E. K. MUSPEATT ON TAB. LAND QUESTION.

A meeting of the Waterloo and District Women's Liberal Association was held on Tuesday evening in the Olive Hall, Waterloo, Mrs. Spencer Leese in the chair,for the purpose of hearing an address from Mr. E.K Muspratt on "The Land Question." Mr.Muspratt critcised Mr. Gladstone's land purchase scheme of 188 G, contending that the objection to small land- owners was the same as to large ones. Both poc- keted the increased value of the land, which was created not by them but by the people. The land should be taxed,and owners could not then afford to keep laud vacant. Afr.Goschen had done everything to throw taxation on to the industry of the people. But, by means of dipping his hand into the pockets of the people, by taxing industry, he was able to make reductions elsewhere "in aid of the rates." He hoped his hearers would be able to judge between the speeches of the two groat parties.

SINGULAR SCENE IN A ST. lIRLRNB POLICR COURT. At St.llelens,on Monday,a rough-looking woman, named Margaret Ford, who had been many times convicted, was charged with wilful damage to a closet in the police cell to the amount of 13. Just before the case came on prisoner,who had exhibited a great deal of excitement, pulled off her clog, and threw it across the court at the constable who had arrested her on another charge. The missile hit an old lady on the right hand,but missed the constable. Prisoner Ines held down by three other constables, who were in the dock, and a strict watch was kept over her. During the hearing prisoner made use of very bad language,and said that she couldn't do any- thing else. It was a day she was having. She had nothing else to do. and she wouldn't play with her feet. (Laughter.)—Uhief Constable Wood asked for the maximum penalty on the charge for which she was arrested, and the charge of wilful damage was not proceeded with.--She was committed for a month.
UMBRICLLLEI ItECOVERET.-7. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-at. Warrington.—Advt. STRANGE DEATH AT Sr. HELENS.

lir. Brighouse held an inquest at L2t. Helens Town Hall, on Wednesday, on the body of James O'Kelly, a labourer, 35 years of age, who lived at ' Havannah, Parr. From the evidence it appeared 1 that on Christmas Eve O'Kelly was found in War- rington Old-road, in an unconscious state. He was taken to the Providence Hospital, but could not at any time give an account of how he received his I injuries, which consisted of a fracture to the scalp, injuries to the back and legs, and a number of small bruises.—Dr. Fred Knowles, who had made a post-mortem examination, said that the primary cause of death was the injuries. The injuries could not have been caused by falling ; they were the result of direct violence. There was no sign of his having been run over, but they might have been caused by being run against by a cart.—The jury found that death was due to the injuries re- ceived, but there was no evidence to show how he cameby those injuries, and an open verdict was returned. SUDDEN AND SINGULAR DEATH OF A #VOMIN. An inquest was held by Mr. Brighouse at the Bull's Head, Parr, St. Helens, on Wednesday, touch- ing the death of Susanna Walker, thirty-one years of age, who lived with her husband in Fleet-lane, but died under singular circumstances. On Friday afternoon last deceased, her Is usband, and five children, partook of some cockles, which the hus- band did not think were very fresh. She was getting ready about six o'clock to go to St. Helens when she complained ot severe pains in the stomach. Walker gave his wife some whisky, and this appeared to relieve her, but abcut midnight she became worse, and died.—Dr, Reid, who was called in to attend her at half-past twelve, stated that she was dying, almost pulseless, and in a com- plete state of collapse. He prescribed brandy, and heard the history of the case. He was unable to form an opinion as to the cause of death. He did not think she had been poisoned by the cockles, or the others would have been affected. The symp- toms were consistent with death from an irritant poison.—The jury returned a verdict that death was due to, natural causes, but as to the precise cause there was not sufficient evidence to show. MR. LEGH M.P., .A.T HA.YDOCK. A public meeting in support of Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P. for Newton Division, whose return is being opposed by Mr. W. Neill, the Liberal candidate, was held in the Colliery Schools, Haydock, on Wednes- day night. Mr. A. H. Evans presided. A resolution expressing unabated confidence in the present Government, and conveying thanks to Mr. Legh, M.P., for his services, was carried. It was moved by Mr. T. D. Grimke-Drayton, seconded by Mr. G. Walden, and supported by Mr. C. B. F. Borron, C.C. Mr. Legh, M.P., subsequently addressed the meeting. He said he did not intend to go into all the reasons why they should support the present Government, nor did he intend to go into the reasons why trade had improved under that Government. He found when Mr. Gladstone was in office 1882, the total value of exports and imports,in the United Kingdom was £1,710,000,000; at the end of 1886, after nearly 5 years of office this total had dwindled to no less a sum than £618,000,000, which left a deficit of no less than 101 million pounds. The figures for five years of the present Government were, in 1887, , .£643,000,000 and in 1891 they had risen to £744,000,000 ' • showing an increase on the five years of not less than .£101,000,000. He then proceeded to speak of the Irish question, and alluded to the suggested abolition of winning royalties. The usual votes of thanks concluded the proceedings.

CONFERENCE OF BIND OF ROPE SOCIETIES AT RUNCORN. Last night a conference of delegates from the bands of hope and other temperance societies in the town was held in Bethesda Schoolroom, for the purpose of considering the Bill to pro- hibit the sale or delivery of intoxicating liquor to any person under the age of 16 years of age. • The Rev. John Simpson presided, and there was a , large attendance. After a discussion it was unanimously decided to petition Parliament in favour of the Bill. In connection with the same sub- ject Mr. B. Bisbrown has given notice that at the next meeting of the Board of Commissioners he will move the following resolution :—" That the Chairman be author- ised to affix the seal of the Board to petitions tO both houses of Parliament in favour of the Sale of Intoxicat- ing Liquor to Children Bill, whereby it is proposed to prohibit the sale or delivery of any description of intoxi- cating liquor to any person apparently under the age of 16 years."

GUARDIANS.

His Honour Judge Foulkes at Runcorn County Court on Saturday, heard an interpleader case from Kingsley, in which Sarah Starkey was the claim- ant, the Guardians of Runcorn Union were the execution creditors, and John Starkey, husband of claimant, was the execution debtor. The case was brought to recover .87 158. 4d which had been paid into court by claimant to avoid a sale of furniture by the Guardians, to meet a demand of £5 145., for relief granted to Henry Starkey, Kingsley, father of the execution debtor, for which he had given a promissory note due last June. Mr. Ashton represented the Guar- dians, as clerk to the Union.—Mrs. Starkey stated that she was married in 1884, and lived on her father's farm, who stocked the place. She nad also money of her own, with which a number of articles of furniture had been purchased. The sum she had received would come out of her fortune. Her husband had no money when they were married, in fact she had to nay the marriage ex- penses. She also discovered that the ring was not paid for, and she had to find the money.—By Mr. Ashton: Her husband was the tenant of the farm. A quantity of the furniture had since been sold by her father und a distraint of rent.—Claimant's story was uncorroborated and his Honour said the law now was that anything she had became her own after marriage. But in that case everything purchased was by money in her father's pos- session, and the things were handed to her husband. He was afraid the claim must fail as the goods were gifts to her husband.—Judgment was given for the execution creditors.

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
"By AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT."

The appeal of the Runcorn Technical Education Committee for donations in aid of the proposed Technical Institute is a document full of interesting facts. There is no attempt at advocacy; the facts are left to tell their own unvarnished tale, and a careful and thoughtful perusal of these facts leads to the conclusion that he Committee ought not,and assuredly will not, "appeal in vain." During the past winter 200 students have been instructed in twelve subjects, all of the highest importance, and the success thus far achieved may be taken as an augury that with a thoroughly equipped institution and able masters, still greater achievements would be wrought. The establishment of a Technical Institute such as that projected would uni‘ ers- ally improve the educational facilities of the town, which at the present time is much behind the age in matters of education. Parents desirous of giving their sons a good educa- tion would not be put to the necessity of sending them to Liverpool at great expense, and those parents who are unable to afford that expense would have at their own doors a school where their boys of talent and industry might gain knowledge, which if properly applied, would win them positions of influence and honour. The Institute will be an untold blessing to the children of the working classes.

There is another phase to the question. If Eng- land is to maintain her commercial supremacy, her sons will have to receive a much higher education than they do at present. If we are to compete with the Continental nations in the markets of the world our workmen must receive an education and a tech- nical training more on a level with that of Germany and the Technical Institute will be the first and important step for Runcorn in this direction. Up to the present time Mr. Brunner has conditionally promised ..C5OO, and Mr. Speakman £5O. Who will swell the list ?

Mr. Brunner M.P., was present at a meeting of the Ancient Order of Foresters, at North wich on Satur- day, on the occasion of a presentation, and he de- livered an admirable address on State pensions. He evidently does not view Mr. Chamberlain's scheme with favour, and pointed out several of its faults. He is a great believer in Friendly Societies and has more faith in self help than in State aid.

The concert of the Runcorn Tonic Sol Fa classes was an unqualified success on Monday evening from every point of :view' and was alike creditable to conductor and pupils. These classes have been the means of disseminating s knowledge of music to hundreds, who perhaps otherwise would have re- mained IR ignorance of the sacred art to the end of their days and as Mr. Speakman remarked in his ad- mirable speech all honour is due to Mr. llolford for the noble work he had performed. I echo the wish that increased success may attend the classes.

div.head: CLASSES. ANNUAL PERFORMANCE.
div.p: CLASSES. ANNUAL PERFORMANCE.

The tenth session of these classes, of which Mr. John Holford is the principal, was brought to a successful and appropriate termination on Monday evening by the performance in Runcorn Public Hall, of Mr. W. 11. Birch's beautiful cantata " The wreck of the Argosy." The pupils were assisted by a num- ber of former members of the classes, and the chorus consisted of 180 voices. There was a large and appreciative audience. The cantata is the musical unfolding of a dramatical love story and the personations were Lellie Marston, (daughter of a village innkeeper), Miss Heatherington ; Harry Stanchion, (barrister), Mr. E. Worrell ; Ralph Har- man, (pirate), Mr. J. Leathwood ; Alice Harman, (sister of Ralph), Miss Cullis ; Will Sharp, (coast- guard), Mr. E. Evans; chorus of villagers, sailors, pirates, &c. The accompainists were : Pianoforte, Mr. C. Le Couteur ; organ, Mr. Harry Pope. The overture, arranged for a pianoforte duet and organ, is a charming composition, and was performed with admirable skill and effect, Miss Pope assisting at the piano. Then came the opening chorus, " Sweet spring, all hail," and in this, and through- Out the whole work the choir performed their by no means light or easy task in a manner that was alike higely creditable to their musical attainments and to their conductor and teacher, Mr. Holford. The soloists comprised an array of local talent,which the audience was not slow to recognise and appreciate ; and the various recitations and songs were rendered with splendid effect, and each vocalist bad the honour of a recall in some part of the cantata. In fact the whole performance was one of unusual excellence, and the attention and interest of the audience was maintained to the end, with only one interval, for the distribution of prizes. In introducing Mr. P. Speakman, C.C., to perform this duty, Mr. Holford mentioned that that gentleman was far from well and had come from London at great per- sonal inconvenience. (Applause.) Mr. Speakman said it gave him great pleasure to be there that night, and to do what he had endeavoured to do at all times, all he could do for the interest of Run- corn. He thought they would agree with him that a word of congratulation would not be at all out of place to Mr. Holford for the indefatigable way in which he had carried out the teaching of the tonic sol-fa system, I and the brilliant success be had achieved. Mr. Speak- man paid gP a .hi h com li meat to the chorus of that even- ing for ti admirable performance, and said that gathering celebrated the termination of the tenth annual session of the singing class. As he was most heartily in I , sympathy with every movement which had for its object ' the social ,moral ,or intellectual improvement of his fellows so he was pleased to be there that evening to do what he could to show his approval of this good work. (Applause.) Mr. Holford said a summary of the attendances at the classes for the past ten years showed a gradual increase, until last year there were in attendance at all classes 131 students, and they hoped for greater success in the future. Of these 22 had passed in the junior stage, 26 in the elementary, sin elementary theory, and 7 in the intermediate stage. div.head: SHIP CANAL. LIVERPOOL AND THE PROPOSED RITES AND CHARGES.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL. LIVERPOOL AND THE PROPOSED RITES AND CHARGES.

A meeting of the Council of the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce was held on Wednesday, when a schedule of objections and recommendations was submitted in refer- ence to the proposed maximum rates, tolls, and charges by the Manchester Ship Canal Company, as submitted to the Board of Trade. It was pointed out that these maxi- mum rates for which powers were sought were higher in various instances than the rates charged by the North- Western Railway Company, and it was urged that canal rates should not be so high as railway rates, the main- tenance of a canal being less costly than a railroad. The proposed station and service terminal charges were also , objected to, and the President,Mr. M'Arthur, stated that while the Chamber was determined to take up this battle against the Company to prevent it getting such powers as were sought in the bill, they would expect the general public who were interested in the matter to supply the sinews of war. Mr. Thorburn also remarked that there must be some feeling of disappointment amongst the Manchester people, who expected to get their goods carried for almost next to nothing.

STRIKE OF NAVVIES-AT NORTON. A strike of navyjes of somewhat serious proportions took place at the Big Field, Norton, near Runcorn, on Monday morning. At this place the canal cutting has to go to a great depth, and six- steam navvies were engaged scooping up the earth. Under the old regime the numerous men needed in conjunction with these machines were paid at the rate of 6d. per hour, but the work has now come under the control of Mr. John Jackson, of Westminster, who has secured from the company the contracts for making the canal from Old Quay to Randles Creek, and it was announced by his representative that the rate of pay in future would be 51d. per hour. The men interested, about 200,at once struck work,and they induced their comrades who were receiving a lower, but satisfactory rate, to also throw up their tools. As one navvy remarked to the writer, they had to throw them up or have them knocked from their hands. The men formed into procession, and walked four deep to Runcorn, and when that place was reached the total number on strike had swollen to 800. During the afternoon knots of seven or eight navvies were standing about the streets, but they kept orderly and of good behaviour. The men claim that the labour they have to do merits the rate of pay they have been receiving, as the material they are cutting through is very difficult to work, and they are often up to the knees in mud. Another grievance was the refusal of the contractor to convey the men to their work. As the men have no union it was not expected that the dispute would be of long duration, and an im- minent collapse of the strike appeared highly probable on Tuesday morning. Sufficient men returned to work to start two steam navvies on their earth-tearing mission, but their comrades quickly arrived on the scene and forcibly drove them away. Afterwards a police sergeant and a number of constables patrolled the neigh- bourhood, but no other disturbance happened. On Wednesday morning, Mr. Jackson's representative was at the Old Quay, where the "mail train "to convey men to their work was in waiting, and he informed the men that they could go to work if they wished at the rate of pay fixed upon, and if they did not take advantage of this offer other men would be engaged and they must go away. The "mail train" was quickly filled and the strike was at an end. The men have thus accepted the masters' terms. It is stated that the stoppage was a loss of £l6O a day to the contractor, but the accuracy of the state- ment cannot be vouched for.

At the advanced age of 80 years, Mr. Samuel Taylor, of Greenway-road, Runcorn, passed quietly away shortly after one o'clock on Wednesday after- noon. Death was due to senile decay. A native of the town, Mr. Taylor commenced work as a rope maker when nine years of age, and continued in this occupation for some years. Subsequently for a long peiiod he had charge of the slate yard of Messrs. Samp- son Potter and Dutton, and in 1884 he took in hand the,. making of boxes for the firm of Messrs. Hazlehurst and Sons, soap manufacturers. In 1890 having worked for 70 years, he retired and has passed the brief portion of life left to him freed from business cares. Mr. Taylor was a devoted member of the Weslevan denomination. He joined the Methodist Church in 1831, and the regu- larity of his attendance to his religious duties is attested by the fact that he had in his possessicn every class ticket from the time ho was received on trial up to the last quarter—no less a record than 60 years of faithful adherence to the cause. For a long period he was a Sunday School teacher, and he held the distinction of being the oldest class leader in Runcorn circuit. His personal knowledge of Wesleyanism in this part of the country extended over 70 years, and his reminiseences of the toast struggles and successes, and the changes that had taken place, were told with delight and were- highly interesting and entertaining. He was one of the earnest band of Methodists who crossed the Mersey by the ferry every Sunday, and who were the means of establishing the Wesleyan Society that now flourishes there. The deceased gentleman was held in high esteem not only by the Wesleyan body but by all who knew him, for his upright, consistent and God fearing life. He leaves to mourn his death a daughter and two sons, who following in their father's footsteps, are devoted members of the Wesleyan denomination. One of the sons is the Rev. J. H. Taylor who is at present in charge of the Shotley Bridge and Consett circuit, Durham. The funeral takes place at Runcorn Cemetery this after- noon.
WARRINGTON SHOP ASSISTANTS' ASSOCIA TI ON. CONCERT AND SOCIAL GATHERING.

In connection with the above-named Association a concert and social gathering were held on Thurs- day eveting in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey- at. There was a large attendance. Mr. T. Morris pre- sided. . .

The CHAIRMAN, in his opening remarks, said that the last time he was on that platform they had not got the half-holiday. Now they had it. (Applause.) There was great cause for the assistants of the town to be cheered by their success, but while being cheered he would beg of them not to lose their respect towards their employers, and not talk as though it was only right that the employers should give way at once, but feel thankful that they so cordially fell in with the request that had been made to them as regarded the half-holiday. (Hear. hear.) He asked therm also to so spend their half-holiday so that they should be both physically and morally better, and more cheer- ful in performing their duties during the other .51 days of the week. Let their employers see that they were thankful for the holiday and appreciated the kindness that granted it. He felt convinced that not a single shop-keeper in the tiwn had lost a penny by granting the half-holiday, while he would no doubt be better in his own health for he had the half-holiday as well as his assistants. Mr. Morris then referred to the question of early closing throughout the week, and urged the as- sistants to endeavcur to get all shop-keepers to close their shops at seven o'clock. He was thankful for the half-holiday, but he should be more thankful still when they had secured early closing in addition. (Applause.) In the course of the evening, Mr. W. Rol:tents moved a vote of thanks to the tradesmen who had so kindly , assisted in bringing about the half-holiday. This was seconded by Mr. KENT, and heartily passed. The musical part of the programme was carried through in a very successful manner. The most conspi- cuous performances were those on the concertina by Profesaor F. W. Malburn. fig imitations of the sounds of a farm yard were particularly clever, but at all his appearances the Professor was loudly applauded, and often recalled. The programme also included a violin solo lsy Mr. R. H. Pearson, songs by Mr. H. Wahineton Mrs. Pearson, Mr. T. Simpson (Manchester), aneMiss' ricton, and " eccentricities " by Messrs. div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF MR, T. YATES, or
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF MR, T. YATES, or
PADGATE.

Mr. Thomas Yates ,a well-known resident of Pad gate, died very suddenly yesterday morning. Mr. Yates rose about seven o'clock and went to fetch his letters from the letter box at his garden gate, Ile returned to the house and sat down to break- fast. He had not sat down long when be removed from his seat to a sofa, and almost immediately ex- pired. Dr. White was at once sent for, and, on arriving, he gave it as his opinion that death was the. result of heart disease. Mr. Yates was 62 years of age,. and leaves a wife and two daughters, one of whom is married. In his younger days he was employed on the. farm of the late Mr. Barber, in Wash-lane, Latchford. Ire afterwards rented a farm en his own account for many years at Orford, and also commenced business aa a corn dealer, in which he was very fortunate. A few years ago he built a commodious house at Padgate,and, I retiring from farming, he went to live there. He, how- ever, continued actively in his business as a corn dealer- till his death. Mr. Yates was never prominently identi- fied with any public work, though he was, we believe for some time, an office holder in connection with Fad. gate Church, which he attended.

MORE THIRVISH BOYS. At the borough police court on Monday, Percy Quinn, Pilkington's Yard, son of William Pilkington, the lad's ago being stated as 10, hut by his mother as 9, and Patrick Ward, aged 11, son of James Ward, 11 Stanley- street, were charged with stealing from the Market Hall, some time between 7 p.m. on the 20th inst.., and the following morning, three meat pies, and a pair of spec- tacles. value is 61. the property of William Cox, also a -quantity of cheese and sweets, value 29., the property of Mrs. Li wless.—Detective-Sergeant Monaghan deposed to complaints tieing made to him about the lads by the Prosecutors, as to the thefts, lie said Quinn was in the habit of concealing himself in the Market Hall at night and sleeping there, in order to steal. He had not been at home since Tuesday night.—Chief Constable Hunt said something would have to be done with Quinn's father. If he resorted to correction of the boy it was in the most brutal manner. Recently he corrected him be giving bim a kick on the head and another somewhere else, and the lad scrambled away in his shirt through the window and hid himself fir a considerable Om.. D.S. Monaghan: He has the mark on his hip now.—Mr. Hunt said the lad had been most brutally treated. The matter would be taken up now, and he would see if he could get hold of the father.—ln reply to the Mayor, Mr. Hunt sail the officer for the society for the prevention of exuelty to children, had been acquainted with the case. —Both lads were ordered to he detained to he locked up till 8 that night, Quinn not to he birched, lie not being in a fit con iition for this, but Ward to have six strokes with the birch rod.

At the Warrington Borough C mrt, on Tuesday, Messrs. Rylands Bros., Limited, were charged with hay- ing worked eight boys after six o'clock at nlg,hl- on the 17th March. Mr. Jones, factory inspector, prosecuted, and Mr. A. Browne defended. Richard Johnsen, assist- ant inspector of factories, stared that he visited Messrs. Rylands works on the night in question between twenty minutes and half-past seven Yelock. and he found very many young persons working in dift.n.ent parts of the works. He took the names of eight of thin. None of the eight attempted to get away,hut many of the others ran away across a yard and tried to get over the bound- ary wall, but were driven back by a policeman who was on the other site. Some of the boys told witness that they had been working from six in the morning, and that they had worked till eight o'clock on two other ni,hts that week.—Mr. Browne admitted the facts as stated by the inspector. That was one of these cases in which his clients were under a penalty to 'finish certain work. The boys also worked voluntarily. His instructions were that neither the directors -nor anybody in the office had the slightest knowledoe of what was being done, the manager having caused tbe horst() work through a very heavy compul- sion to completethe work. He asked the Bench to be as lenient as possible, and promised that the offence would not be committed again.-.-4r. R. Garnett (chairman) said the case was a clear one, and the Bench were glad that no defenco was set up tiaat was at all unreasonable. 'There had certainly been a breach of the law which ought to be errferced, and they would impose a fine of Ze and costs in regard to the first case, and the defend- ants would have to pay the costs in each of the other MICA.

div.head: gATUR DA Y, APRIL: Mi 1'8921'
div.p: gATUR DA Y, APRIL: Mi 1'8921'

Mr. Browne appeared for the defence.—P.S. Booth said on the 11th inst., there was a sale of sheep and cattle at the Ring-o-Bell's, Daresbury, and the auctioneer gave instructions that according to the Act of Parliament the animals must be slaughtered in Cheshire, and not taken out of the couuty alive, and he notified that they were to be taken to the Stag Inn, Walton, prior to being slaughtered. Mr. Cross bought several sheep and a cow and three calves, and they were taken to the Stag Inn. That day witness found that four of them had been taken to Warrington by Warburton and Kelly, alive, and next day that two of them had been brought back alive by Kelly.—Thos. Warburton stated that after the sale Mr. Cross went home instructing him and Kelly to take the sheep in a trap to the Stag Inn, to have them slaughtered.—They took Clem, and afterwards when they went into the stable to bring them out to be slaugh- tered it was dark, and they could not distinguish by the candlelight which were Mr. Cross's sheep from others that were there, the sheep being badly marked. They did not know what to do. and were afraid ef slaughter- ing the wrong sheep, so they took four away alive in a cart, to Warrington. When they got there, they saw they had got two wrong sheep. Mr. Cross had then gone out of the town, and early in the morning witness sent Kelly back with the two sheep.—Kelly corroborated, and Mr. Cross gave evidence as to his being from home and his having nothing to do with the sheep being removed alive.—The Bench considered the case privately for a short time, and then the Chairman said they con- sidered the cases proved. Mr. Cross ought to have seen that he sent proper men with the sheep, on the 11th inst., and as to that date he would he fined £1 and costs, and Warburton and Kelly would be fined 10s. and costs each, and as to the 12th inst., they would be fined the costs each. REFUSING TO QUlT.—Robert Pearson was chargediwith refusing to quit the house of Mrs. Fanny Maddock, the Stag Inn, on March 30th on bAng requested by her to do so. Mr. Browne appeared for the prosecution. He said the defendant and others went in and had a quart of beer amongst them, and broke a chair and when Mrs. Maddock complained, the defendant used some horrible language to her. She told him she would not have this and he must go out. An old man remonstrated with him and he knocked him down, and when the landlady told him he ought to be ashamed of himself, again used mast horrible language. She then sent for the police to eject him.—The facts haying been proved, the defendant admitted his guilt, but denied breaking the chair.—Mr. • Browne: We don't say it was you. Somebody did.—The defendant was fined 53. and costs. BREACHES OF THE GAME Laws—William RUSIRZt, of Warrington, was charged that on being searched by constables on the 31st of March, on his coming from cer- tain land at Latchford where, it was suspected he had been in search of game he was found in possession of a net and pegs used for taking and killing game.
