div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.

We have had a plentiful crop of surprises during the season, but surely the climax was reached on Saturday last. According to the prophets four Cup finals went utterly wrong, but one hardly knows which of the four created the greater astonishment. Look at those results : —Lancashire Cup : Bury,two coals; Blackburn Rovers, none. Manchester Cup : Ardwick, four goals ; Bolton Wanderers. one. Staffordshire Cup Burton Swifts,two goals ; Aston Villa, 1. Yorkshire Cup : flunslet, three goals, three tries ; Leeds, nothing.

Many persons have assumed that Hunslet were much the heavier team in the Yorkshire Cup tie last week. It may, therefore, be interesting to note that Hunslet averaged 12st. 11b. a man, and Leeds list. 131 b., or a majority of 21b. only per man in favour of the Park- siders. Hunslet were notable for the general level of the weights, seven being just over 12st., and only two over I3st. Co the other hand, five Leeds men drew the scale at over 13st., and the others were more or less light weights.

The victory of Hunslet in the Yorkshire final was immensely popular everywhere except with the direct supporters of the Leeds club, One well-known Wake- field man was heard to say on the field that he was as pleased RS if his own team were the conquerors. The same feeling was prevalent in Huddersfield, Bradford, Halifax, &c., circles. The truth is Leeds people have got altogether too " toney "and almighty to please other Yorkshire people, and the modesty of the Flunslet club has shone all the more resplendently by contrast. [he result is a severe lesson to Leeds, but it may be useful.

Three of the League clubs figured in gloriously in Cup ties on Saturday. They must be tired of the game or they would surely never have gone down as they did. Aston Villa, Bolton Wanderers, and Blackburn Rovers were all beaten by " minor lights," and there is no , doubt that one and all calculated in the morning of hav- ing a cup in the evening. But" there' many a slip 'twixt cup and lip," and the favourites were defeated in each case. All honour to the three winners.

The Lague compotition i 3 now practically at an end, for only the match between Burnley and Sunderland re- mains to be played, and this can only do two things— put Burnley in frotot of Everton or give Sunderland a record in the matter of League points, the Wearside team now equalling the number obtained oy Preston North End in 1.883, blot of course they -have played four more snatches.

Some enterprising, and veracious correspondent caused a genuine scare in Leeds and district on Friday night by telegraphing an account of an "alarming " accident, in whichhalf the Leeds team had been half drowned and "seriously injured " on tha river Nidd, at Knares- borough. The only foundation for the sensation was a " dousing, " which Donaldson received as a result of "crab-catching." The author of the exaggeration would have had a *arm time of it had certain Leeds officials been able to lay hands upon him.

-- St. Elphin's (Warrington) Association Football club have, during the season, played 23 matches, of which they have won 9, drawn 3, and lost 11, scoring 32 goals against their opponents 64. In the first four matches 29 goals were piled against them which was a great draw- b ick, but they have wr,rked hard since and have de- feated all the Association Clubs in the borough ;—Grain- mar School. Cricket Club A.F.C., Orford Barracirs, and what was considered the leading club, Warrington As- sociation. The Rev. T. W. Cook has been the mainstay of the team.

div.p: MISCRLLANROTIS.

A meeting of the Council of the County Bowling Association vras held at Wigan, on Saturday, for the pur- pose of drawing ties for the first series of competidons and for other business. Mr. J. J. Meakin (iersal), pre- sident, was in the chair, and the following affiliated districts were represented :—Withington, Warrington, Leigh. Broughton, Newton, Wigan, Sefton Park, Hinds- ford, Barlow Moor. and Harpurhey. The draw was , then proceeded with, and resulted as follows :—Sefton Park v. Hindsford, at Newton-le-Willows ; Warrington v. Wigan, at Leigh ; Newton-le-Willows v. Leigh, at Warrington; Broughton v. Didshury, at Croft's Bank ; Withington •. Cherlton-curn-Hardy, at Harpurhey ; Croft's Bank o. Barlow Moor, at Stretford ; Old Trafford v. Urmston, at Withington ; Stretford v. Harpurhey, at Broughton; Aigburth (Livcrpool). Walton (Liverpool), and Denton Private Club, Limited, to be drawn by seb- -11 committee as soon as preliminaries are completed. All ! contests to be concluded by 14th May, and in the event of any two clubs failing to agree upon a date, the same to be communicated to the sub-committee prior to the 10th of May, and their decision to be final. A sugges- tion for holding the annual championship contest in July, instead of Ssptember, as hitherto, was adjourned.

div.head: TERRIBLE WIFE MURDER AT LEEDS.
div.p: TERRIBLE WIFE MURDER AT LEEDS.

Holbeck. an industrial -suburb of Leeds, was the scene of a shocking wife murder on Saturday night. The murderer is a mechanic named Henry Pickerimr',twenty- nine years of age, who, with his wife, aged twenty- three, to whom he was married only three months ago, lived with his parents in Ozar-st. Fallowing his wife upstairs about half-past eight, he seems to have thrown her on the bed, and with a huge new butcher's knife cut her throat right across, severing all the main arteries. His father, hearing her screams, went to b!..,r aid ;hut she died in twenty minutes. Meanwhile, the accused took to his heels,but was captured about a mile away. When charged he said, "It's all through jealousy. She kept saying she would go and leave me, but now no one else shall have her." Although Pickering's parents are held in great respect, he himself bears a bad character.

RUGBY. WARRINGTON v. SWINTON. Following their three victories at Eagtertide, the Warriugtonians journeyed to Swinton on Saturday to piay off the ieturn fixture. The prospects of Warring-
:on again accounting for the "collier boys" were indeed
remote when it was found that neither Evans nor Web-

ster could assist them. On the other hand, Swinton had a full team, their corfibination being improved by the assistance of Tom flaslam, the Dukinfleld back. A large crowd witnessed the match, and the Warringtonians

div.head: did not lack support, nearly 200 journeying with our
div.p: did not lack support, nearly 200 journeying with our

local team. Mr. Leigh Clare, the Unionist candidate for the Eccles division, kicked off amidst a hurricane of ap- plause, and the kick being met by Turner, Pearson re- sponded to Heesom, whose return found touch at the home quarter flag. The visitors' forwards rushed to the line, Jolley and Ashton being conspicuous, and in some loose play the oval was sent over, but Valentine pluckily, though injudiciously, ran the oval out, Heesom pressing him when he punted. Valentine again eased the attack a little, but in trying to repeat the dose a third time, John Bate made no mistake, and from a scrimmage the Bates got the better of Bumby and Brock- bank, and some pretty passing between the former saw Heesom kicking to Valentine, the Swinton captain mak- Inc his mark. Boscow met the kick in true style, and Warrington maintained the pressure, though their finishing essays lacked finish. Pearson attempted to get away, but he acted with excellent discretion when he refused to face Turner, and Boscow again forcing the Swintonians back, Flaslarn had a handful when Donohue, Randle's, and Thornilev dribbled up to the home quarters, the home back kicking into touch near his lines. Short rushes by the Swinton forwards reached the half-way flag, Murray and Bothwell head- lug the way. Bumby essayed to clear, and although he managed to evade the vigilance of James Bate, Turner made no mistake with his man. Better results came of a run and pass by Murray to Chapman, and the game was drangerously near the visitors' line. Some passing by Brockbank, G. Sharplee, and Bumby saw Jolley tak- ling the latter, and Daniels spoiling Pearson, the Warring- tonians breathed more freely. The Bates and Heesom again passed Well, and James Bate Punting down the open, Haslam was hard pressed, when he punted into touch at his own quarterflag. A mirk to Valentine was the next item,aud Haslam, having a kick charged, the Svrintlon goal appeared at Warrington's mercy. The chance was allowed to slip, and, in response to their over eagerness, a couple of fine runs by Valentine and Pearson were nipped in the bud by 'Boscow and Nevins. A good piece of play by Turner, Buckley, Beeson), and Ashton regained the lost ground, and Warrington were again hard on the attack. Brilliant passing by the home hacks reached half way, and from a line out Jolley got clear away, and, when everyone had predicted that the visitors would at least notch something tangible, a pass forward upset the good run. The home front rank wheeled a scrimmage well, and Warrington fell back on their lines. Again the visitors changed the venue, but Valentine, taking a pass from Brockbank, smartly made off at top speed. Gradually he got clear,and Swintonians in general proclaimed a score for their hero, when Bos- cow grasped the homester and floored him in fine style. Murray next put in a good run, and John Bate and , Knowles became prominent parties in the saving line.' Holmes. Jolley, and Thorniley came away in a body,and managed to reach the half-way flag, the former spoiling Pearson in his effort to get away. Bumby had a narrow shave from a score a minute later, a minor being • con- ceded. Following some fine play by Ashton, Buckley, and Nevins, for their respective sides came is grand run by James Bate, but again the final pass was bad. Swinton passed well, and in the last minute of this half Murray ran and passed to Hallam, who scored a clever try, and at the interval the homesters led by a try and a minor to nil. Warrington assumed the aggressive al- most immediately the kick-off had taken place, Jolley, Bandies, and Boscow all helping to bring about this. The Warrington custodian and Valentine exchanged kicks, with advantage to the hornesters, and from some loose play at neutral ground Valentine sailed away until Ashton floored the Swinton captain when on the verge of scoring. Betteritick attended an effort by Winterbottom, for, runining to the line, he passed to G. Shareles, the latter scoring, but Hasiam failed to augment. Follow- ing the drop-out some pretty cross-dribbling by liuckley liand Jolley was neuralised by Bumby, but the latter's pasts was a shade forward. Valentine found the tackling too good to allow him many opportunities, and although the visitors broke away, the cleverness of Pearson and Murray did not allow of relief for a length- ened period. The last-named put in a fine run and pass to Valentine, for that player to gain a ridiculously easy try between the posts, and taking the place himself, he had no difficulty in augmenting. Warrington were at the Swinton end on the restart, a free kick bringing about this, but a couple of punts by Valentine sufficed for the homesters reaching the Warrington quarters. Boserew again tackled the home centre finely, and Ban- dies following up a kick by Heescan collared Winter- bottom at half-way. Splendid passing by the Bates, Heesom, and Nevins, did not gain much ground, whilst on the other hand Bumby stole away from a scrimmage oppesite the grand stand, and, in conjunction with Bothwell, scored a fourth try, a confident appeal for pass forward being over-ruled. Five minutes from time Warrington attacked the Swinton goal in a marvello,a manner, considering the rapid pace at which the game had been carried on. A minor was notched, and from a forward rush Flaslam collared Jolley under the posts, Final score :—Swinton,l-3-1; Warrington, 0-0-1. Teams :--Warringten : 3. Boscow, back: W. Nevins, F. Beeson), and W. Daniels, three-quarter backs: James Bate and John Bate, half backs; H. Ashton, Pair Turner, J. Jolley. W. Handles, J. Knowles, J. Holmes, T. Dono- hue, J. T. Thorniley,. and W. Buckley, forwards. Swin- ton: Haslem, hack; W. Winterbottem, J. Valentine, and W. Pearion, three-quarter backs W. Bumby and H. Broachank, half backs; G. Sharpies, A. Sharpies, Hotch- kiss, W. Evans, W. Chapman, T. Hawn, S. Hall, and T. Bothwell, forwards. WALMINGTON A v. SWINTON.—A capital attendance had assembled to see the last of the A team fixtures, when Swinton kicked off against the wind. Glover was the first to he noticeable, the visitors for a time being confined inside their quarters, but after some exchange kicking the Swintonians found relief in conceding a miner. Directly after this Bothwell made a had miss of P. Lawlees's kick, a try almost being obtained. The drop out was of no avail until Fletchkiss and Chapman dribbled to neutral territory, where Westall showed up very prominently, and although Warrington had a try at their mercy the chance was lest, the result being a dead ball, and a second smart attack by J. Lawless forced Smith to touch down. There had been nothing very brilliant in the style of the combatants, but after a very sharp scrimmage, a fine run and pass by P. Law- less enabled his side to attack strongly, and a rush by Westall, Berry, Forster. and Harapson resulted in the former seoring, T. Warburton placing a grand goal. Restarting at midfield. Swinton were quickly forced back by Ashurst and Hammon, but the visiting for- wards, who were playing very, playing very well, soon transferred the warfare into heir opdonents' 25. A grand relief came when Antrohus, J. Lawless, and P. Lawless indulged in a bout of passing, a tall punt by the elder brother pressing the visitors back. Swinton by combined forward play, again attacked, and although Ashnrst relieved once, some strenuous efforts he Harris forced a miner. Warburten, Fligham,iMoly- neang, and Glover soon brought pressure to bear on their npponente, a foolish kick, however, sending the leather dead, Then Swinton had a lorik in, their for- wards exhibiting capital form, Warrington having an anxious time of it. A free kick in a dangerous position looked none too bright, hut the attempt failed, and Warburton, Westall, and Higharn at oncerot the leather right away to the other end, where P. Lawless seizing the hall pet in a splendid peee of work. Bothwell mulled, and Threadgold getting hold, ran in stronely for J. Vilarburtnn to place another grand goal, and half- time arrived. Directly afterwards Warrinsrton, by skil- ful passing, broke through the Swinton defence. Antro- bus was was the first to get away, the hall purling through the hands of Lawless, J. Warburton, and Threadgolel, the' latter winding up a splendid piece of play by scoring. The home team, who were playing four three-quarters, indelged in another fine dienla v of passing, but Swinton, emulating the example of their antagonists, reached midfield. Forster, Molrneux, (Novel% and ffigham, persiStsd in the attack on the visitors' citadel, and then Lally threw to P. Law- , less, who ran splendidly to the line, and passed beauti- fully to J. Warburton, who secured a try. Swinton were now hopelessly beaten, a dribble by. Hampson, Berry, Warbarton, and Meyer travelling to the goal , posts. The brothers Lawless were extremely notable in their unceasing 'efforts, whilst Harris, on behalf of the visitors, rendered-yeoman service to his side. After this Swinton pressed. but Ashurst was a tower of strength behind, and nothing further was Scored, Warrington winning by 2-2-5 to 40.0-1. • RUNCORN v. STOCKPORT.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION T. ELLESMERE POET.—The return fixture was played at Ellesmere Port on Saturday last, before about 800 spectators. Ellesmere kicked off with a strong wind in their favour, and play was at once taken down to the visitors' quarters, where some smatt defence on the part of Kincaird was witnessed. Elles- mere continued to press, and experienced hard lines in not scoring, but the Warrington custodian was too quick for them, earning several rounds of applause for the manner in which he cleared. The Warrington men, now _ _ _ _ _

livened up a bit,.and Munn racing down tile field, put in a good shot which the goalkeeper cleared. Half time was called with no score. Mather restarted, but all the efforts of the Warrington forwards to get away were foiled. A long kick by one of the home backs landed the ball in the visitors' goal, and the first point was scored by a combined rush on the part of the Ellesmere forwards, an appeal for "hands," being disallowed. Play continued for the most part in the Warrington quarters, some dirty play on the part of an Ellesmere forward causing him to receive a caution from the referee. From a pass across the field, Nicholls scored the second goal for Ellesmere, time being called soon after,with the score standing, Ellesmere Port 2, Warrington nil. For the visitors both backs, Kincaird and Davies, Phillips, centre half, and Fennellv, forward, played well.

• WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION RESERVB v. WARRINGTON 1 NORTH END —This match took place on .the Arpley ground, Dutton kicking off for Warrington against a strong breeze. The visitors had the benefit of the open- ing exchanges the right way of working the ball well up field, but were returned by Mather. T. Mather and Lavall next did a neat passing run, but the final effort went wide. Eventually Dutton, gaining possession in midfield, made tracks for the North End's goal, finishing up by scoring a good goal. The visitors' left were now prominent, but Neild returned, when the Reserve made an attack on the visitors' citadel. Half-time, Warrington 1 goal, North End nil. 11,:sta.rtictg,,, the Reserve played rather loose for a time, but, settling down to their work, they overpaced their opponents, Mather scoring a second paint. The home right wing next had a shy, Jones passing t) Dutton,the latter player notching a third goal for the Reserve. After a short interval of even play, the Reserve again took up the running, T. Mather scoring a fourth' thus ending a poor game by Reserve 4, goals' North End nil.

div.head: DISSOLUTION.
div.p: THE DISSOLUTION.

Mr. Balfour has privately informed a political friend in the House of Commons that a general election will certainly take place this year. A London correspondent states that the Government have made preparathns for dissolving at any time, writs for all the constituences having been ready for more than a vveek.
THE WOMAN'S SUFFRAGE DIVISION\.

In the Division on Wednesday upon the second read- ing of the Woman's Suffrage Bill, the majority which voted against Sir A. Rota's motion consisted of 65 Con- servatives, 81 Liberals, 7 Nationalists, and 24 Liberal Unionists; while the minority included 78 Conservatives 53 Liberals, 10 Nationalists, and 13 Liberal Unionists.

div.p: ILA.RRIA.tiE OF MISS TWYFORD, ST.
11EL ENS.

The old parish church of St. Helens was crowded on Wednesday to "fitness the nuptials of Miss Alice Penrose Twyfortl, only child of Mr. E. P. Twyford, M.D., J.P., St. Helens, and Mr. Andrew Gray, M.D., fourth son of Mr. James Gray, J.P., banker, Dal- keith, N.B. The chancel was nicely decorated with plants, ferns, and flowers. The church was crowded long before the hour appointed, and Mr. B. B. Woodward played several voluntaries on the organ. The bride- groom was attended by his brother (Mr. Wm. Gibson Gray), and at noon the bride arrived and proceeded up the aisle leaning on her father's arm. The bride was attired irba tram gown of rich white satin duchesse, I made with a perfectly plain skirt, the edge trimmed with white chiffon, over, a flounce of satin, ornamented with orange blossoms ; the empire bodice had high puffed sleeves, with ylke and neck trimmed with old fioniton lace, the gift of the bride's mother. She also wore a plain tulle veil wreathed with real orange blossoms, and carried a beautiful bouquet of flowers. She was attended by four bridesmaids —Miss _ _.Dorothy Gamble, Miss ,Edith _ ?liking- _ .

ton, Miss Jessie Gibson, and Miss Jamison— The vicar nf St. Helens (the Rev. J; W. Willink) offici- ated, and the interesting proceedings commenced with the hymn" 0 Father, all creating." The bride was given away by her father. The service concluded with singing," Rest in the Lord from harps above." The party then proceeded to the vestry, where the register was signed, and Mr. and Mrs. Gray left the church to the strains of Mendelssohn's "Wedding March," and amid the usual shower of rice and congratulations. Dr. and Mrs. Twyford afterwards gave a dejeuner at their residence in Ormskirk-st. The presents numbered over 120. During the afternoon Mr. and Mrs. Gray were driven to Edge-hill, wh;re they took train for London, en rears to the Continent.
DARING BURGLARY NEAR ST. HELENS.
PREPARING FOR A BIG HAUL

About three' --------------- On Tuesday morning the Eccleston Park. near St. Helens, the resi- dence of Mr. Daniel M'Kechnie, copper smelter, Widnes, son of Alderman IVPKochnie of St. Helens, was entered by a burglar or burglars. About the hour named Mrs. M'Kechnie heard the door of their bedroom creak, and she awakened Mr. M'Kechnie, who, not thinking anything was amiss, got up and pushed the door to. A few minutes afterwards the nurse rushed in from an adjoining room in great fright, and said there was a man in the house, that she had seen him in her room, and that he had just gone downstairs. Mrs. M'Kechnie immediately put her hand to the electric bell, and Mr. William Newsome soon came on the scone. It was then found that the folding window of the break- fast-room at the back of the house had been prized open, and through this the burglar had entered. Spring cleaning having commenced, the furniture had been removed, so the burglar proceeded to the dining- foom. Here he took up a box of wax vestas and pro- ceeded by their light to search the sideboard for silver. Every case had been opened, and on one or two the wax of the vestas had dropped. After inspecting the contents , and placing them handy for carrying them off he , proceeded upstairs and entered the bedroom ordinarily used by Mr. and Mrs. M'Kechnie. They had, however, gone to the spare room, taking the valuables, some of , which lay upon the dressing-table. The burglar searched the wardrobe, and made Mr. M'Kechnie's best clothes into a bundle. Ho then took a second suit and an ' overcoat. Placing them ready, he tried Mr. M'Kechnie's I door, but finding it dangerous, he crept into the nurse's room on his hands and knees. This was also dangerous, as the nurse was awake, though she lay as quiet as possible, and although a watch lay on the dressing-table, be thought it better to retire' which he did, taking up the clothes, one bundle of which he, however, dropped in his flight. He had not time to call in this dining-roons for the silver, although one solid silver sugar sifter is missing This ha probably put in his pocket during his examina- tion. The neighbourhood soon became alarmed, and the Prescot police were sent for, but the man got clear away. The overcoat is a Chesterfield one, valued at £4. It was apparently Mr. M'Kechnie's hanging the door ta that disturbed the burglar, and caused him to beat a hasty retreat.

- EMILIBSTOWN Carcxfir Cum.—The season in connec- tion with the above club ; was practically opened on Saturday afternoon, when a match was played between teams selected from the players, captained respectively by Scott and Saunders. Last year the club created a satisfactory record, but the present season will find clubs of a far superior calibre on the local ground. The prospects for the season are in every way encouraging, and it is confidently expected that the result will fully justify the efforts put forth by the Committee. A valuable addition to the club is the engagement of "Miller," who last season was associated with Radcliffe as professional, and his exhibition on Saturday, was in all respects perfectly satisfactory. J. Harrison, who last season played for a short time with Warrington has also been retainedchis achievements with the ball, being of so notorious a character, as to need no comment now. The fixtures which should excite the greatest: amount of interest locally are those with Newton, as this year's friendly relations, which for some time have been con- siderably straiued,have been restored between the clubs. Amongst the clubs with which fixtures have been arranged are Leigh, Tvldesley, Pendleton, Cheetham, Nantwich, Southport, Gaston, Club Moor, Wavertee and Golborne. The actual hostilities will commence on Saturday, when Leigh will visit the Earlestown ground, and being captained by the celebrated D. P. Lancashire, an excellent game may be expected. ARCHBISHOP.

The annual Easter vestry meeting in connectioln with the Ohurch of the,. St. James-the-Great, Hay-, dock; was held on Monday night, the proceedings being of the mbst harmonious nature. Mr. Arthur Evans, churchwarden, in the absence of a vicar,was ' voted to the chair, and among those, present were Mr. Edwin Jackson (warden), the Rev. R. S. Bar- tram (curate), Messrs. R. Bradshaw, T. llarrison,G. Walden, J. Cawley, J. Marsh, and J. Matthews.

The Chairman staled that the first business on the paper was rather awkward to MM. It was to propose a vote of thanks to the retiring churchwardens, and considering that his co-warden (Mr. Edwin Jackson) had really borne the brunt of the battle throughout the difficulty in which they had been placed, it Seamed ap, propriate that he alone should be thanked. Mr. Waldan said he had much pleasure in submitting such a resolution to the meeting' as a good deal of im- portant work had been done in the most satisfactory manner.

Mr. freafon seconded, and the resolution was carried unanimously. The next business was the election cif wardens, and Mr. Bradshaw stated that as no vicar was there to elect a vicar's warden, he moved that Mr. Arthur Evans and Mr. Edwin Jackson be appointed for the ensuing year. This was carried. The churchwardens were appointed ais lay representatives. The statement of accounts sub- mitted by Mr. jacksen ihnavecta balanee dn'that church in favour of the wardens of £l9 7s. 51:11' buethere were outstanding ,accounts and a deficiency on the St. Alban's Mission-robm amounting to £45 15s. 2d. altogether, time leaving 4 deficiency of £2el: The accounts were passed. The Chairman then said the parish of Haydock had obtaiaed very great and unenviable notoriety throughout the length and breadth of the country in connection with the recent difficulty about the vicar, and he should like a Proposition to be carried, which he would re'ad. It was a resolution of apology to the Archbishop of York, and in this respect their curate (the Rev., Mr. Bertram) had set them a good example, for where people were in the Wrong, the best thing to do vvas to acknow- ledge it. The resolution was as follows That this 'Meeting of the parishioners of St. James-the-Great, in Haydock, desire to place en record their regret that in the heat of the moment so undesirable a tone prevailed at the meeting held in the National Schools, in reference to the decisionof the Archbishop of Yorkin regard to the •Rev. J. C. Cater ; the meeting also wishes to make such amends as may lie in its power by tendering, as a palish, to his Grace the Archbishop of York, a formal expresaion of regret that disrespect should have been shown to him ; also a most humble and sincre apology for whet occurred." Ils (the chairman) did not think anyone Hneed be ashamed to follow Mr., Bartram's example, and he sincerely hoped that the resolution would be carried. Mr. 13radshaw said that every word oft he resolution fell in with his ideas. He went to that parishioners' meeting with the intention of saying a few words tO Mr. Cater, who had been nominated to the living; but he was en disdusted with the tone which prevailed that he thought it better to get outside as soon as possible. He seconded the resolution, a nd hoped it would be carried unanimously. , The Chairman remarked that he thought the people were .aa guilty as the speakers, but it was done in the heat of the moment, and, as such, it could net be taken really and truly as the feeling of the parishioners of Flaydock. They had, however, obtained an unenviable notoriety by that meeting, and must all take blame to themselves. Mr. Walden did net think they should make their un- enviable. notoriety any better by an apology through the newspapers. Because two or three chose to make fools of themselves it that meeting, he did not see why they should stamp the whole of those present at the meeting as fools, for if thee did pass such a resolution, it would stamp the whole lot of them. In reply to the chairman, Mr. Walden said it was the latter part of the resolution that he objected to. The Chairman said it had gone forth to the world that they were amice`lot at Haydock. He did not care whq ; was responsible for it; but the parish had got the credit of it.

• Mr. Bradshaw said he could not take exception to one word of the resolution. Mr. Walden subsequently agreed to the resolution, and it was carried unanimously. The Chairman intimated that the consecration of the I new church would take place immediately, now that a new vicar had been selected. The Rev.W. .J. Melville, patron of the living, wrote saying :—" I trust indeed that now everything will, go on happily at Flaydock. From what Mr. Bowden says, and from what I hear of him from reliable sources I am sure he will lay himself out to do as much good as possible in Elaynock." The Chairman stated that the new vicar bad visited the parish. Ha supposed Mr. Cater would go to Scotland and take charge of the rectory which Mr. Bowden was leaving. He was glad they had some one appointed at last, and that matters would soon sail ahead with some one at the wlseel. The Rev. Mr. Bowden was a Cambridge I Man, and ordained in England. This concluded the business.

div.head: Ettters to tbt Obttor.
div.p: Ettters to tbt Obttor.
RUNCORN TOWN BAND.

Sir,—A movement is on foot to obtain a set of first class silver-plated instruments for what was formerly known as the Runcorn Volunteer Band, but which is in future to go by the title of Runcorn and District Town and Volunteer Band. I have not vet been able to get any satisfactory information as to who it is intended ' shall have the custody and ownership of these valuable instruments, which are to cost over £2OO. Supposing the bandsmen happened to disagree on some occasion and the Band was broken up, what would become of the instruments? Would each bandman claim his own par- ticular piece of silver plate, or would the bandmaster claim the lot? In my opinion this question ought to ble clearly and definitely settled. As the instruments will be purchased ,•,y money subscribed by the townspeople, it seems only just and right that a Committee of towns- people should be the trustees, and until it is so decided, the money cannot be expected to flow in more rapidly than it is doing. Those inclined to help are sure to button up their pockets until it is made publicly known that the whole affair rests on a sound foundation.— Yours, ONE INTERESTED.

div.head: CORPORATION CONTRACTS: AN IMPORTANT
div.p: CORPORATION CONTRACTS: AN IMPORTANT
QUESTION.

Sir,—lt is an old and true saying that Corporations have no conscience. This has been very forcibly ex- emplified by the august body that represents the Town Hall, Baths and Park Department. They have out of their unfathomable wisdom and with a noble contempt of justice and economy given away the work of re- novating the Council Chamber without having adver- tised or invited tenders for the same, which is distinctly contrary to the regulations. lam told on good author- ity that had such been done the saving to the town would have been considerable. Not only have the Chairman and Committee committed this irregularity, but they allowed the work to be commenced before the minutes were submitted to the General Council. When similar work was done last year, tenders were invited and the lowest accepted and the work was strictly carried out according to specifications. On that occasion the contractor had to wait the formal approval of the Council which involved a delay of two months before the work could be started, which is in marked contrast to the manner in which the work has been given out this year. Now, sir, is such conduct fair either to the other tradesmen or to the ratepayers of the town ? I hope the Council on Tuesday will give an answer, and oblige, " A TOWNSMAN FOR TOWNSMEN."

THE WARRINGTON TORIES AND THEIR PLATFORM SUPPORTERS. Sir,—l find that your Tory contemporary, in its report of the Tory meeting, held on Monday last, paid me the undeserved compliment (?) of classing me amongst the platform supporters. Now you will be a little surprised to hear that I was never inside the hall on the evening in question, and only in the ante-room, where I could get a glimpse of the naeetirig. through the open door for about three minutes. I happened to be passing, along Rylands-street about nine o'clock with a friend who suggested that we should Just look in at the meeting. We walked into the ante- room where I remained for the time before mentioned. However the sample of oratory which Mr. Rentoul was making do duty for argument was quite suffi- cient for me. He was telling his audience that a paid member of Parliament was only on a level with the pauper id the Workhouse; and it was not sur- prising that even Tory working-men didn't care to applaud the statement. I see from the" Guardian " report that he also said that the countries which did pay their members, only gave as much as would pay his (Mr. Rentours) postage, which averaged 30 letters per day (?) Well, at that rate per Parliamentary day it would amount to some £25 per annum. Yet I have seen a published statement that most ot these States pay no less than about £3OO per annum to each of their representatives. But as Mr. Rentoul will doubtless receive due consideration else- where, I leave this specimen to the judgment of your readers, merely remarking that Warrington Toryism must be hard pressed, when two Radicals could not look through the open door to their meeting without being classed as platform supporters in order to swell the num- bers.—Yours, &c., T. BIRCHALL.

THE TORY MEETING AT WARRINGTON. Sir,—l was not able to be at the Tory meeting on Monday. I regret it as lam fond of cheap amusement and I believe there was plenty of it there—tall talk and cheap argument. I should have been delighted to have participated in the pleasure of laughing at the imported Orange wit, and some of our native if feeble futilities. There was much talk of "the foreigner " as contrasted with the sative grown " rising crop," as the Tory candi- date has been called. Now the simple folk who make this complaint against Dr. Houston should, to be con- Went, give up drinking tea and coffee and take to hedge- eaves as being of native production. Let us have the best of everything : Houston and coffee, rather than Pierpoint and hedge-leaves. "Then again Radicals were prepared to swallow any- thing." Jam a Radical, but there is one thing I cannot swallow—a Tory who has swallowed his principles. Here is Mr. Pierpoint asking the working-men of War- rington to vote for him, as a Tory—as a member of the party by whom the working-man was vilified, and sneered at as the" great unwashed," and his claim to the rights of citizenship scornfully rejected as long as it was possible to do so, and finally only conceded to outside pressure and exigencies of party policy. And now the meretricious Tory, after having the measure wrung from him, turns to the working-man and says— see what we did for you ! And begs him to use these rights, which, had the Tory had his way he never would have possessed, to enable the said Tory to ad- vance Privilege above Principle. When a working- man is asked by a Tory for his vote by ballot he should ask that cheeky gentleman—lf he or the Tories as a party ever agitated to sbtain those privileges for him ? Mr. Pierpoint is against the payment of members "because we can get the work done for nothine How often is it that what we get for nothing is worth about prime cost? And there are members there dear at this price, and whom it would pay the country to pay to keep away. Such are those who go there—not to work —but merely for the social distinction it confers. But as to the expense, I would do here as Paddy did with the blanket to make it longer—l would cut some off the top and tack it on to the bottom. I would have a day's shooting among the sinecureists and perpetual pen- sioners, and pay certain useful vocations with the pro- ceeds! In comparing the two candidates lam unfavourably impressed by the fact that both of them arelawyers, and, between you and me, sir, we have the law sufficiently well represented already. But here! would reverse the old proverb which says " Of two evils choose the !east," for I would take the one who stood highest in his profes- sion. Ills amnsing and amazing to hear Mr. R. Pierpoint commended for his public spirit. This good quality may have existed in him, but Mr. Pierpoint has been remarkably successful in disguising the fact. Has Mr. Pierpoint ever tried to serve the town in any capacity? If not, say why not ?—I am, sir, yours, JOHN PEERS.
Penketh, 28th April, 1892. P.S.—How does Mr. Rentoul's " law-abiding Ulster' fit in with their recent threats of pikes, powder. and -trenches, should their legislative wishes be not fulfilled ?

div.head: MR. ROBERT PIERPOINT AND THE WORKING-
div.p: MR. ROBERT PIERPOINT AND THE WORKING-
MEN OF WARRINGTON.

Sir,—! hope that the working-men of Warrington will keep well in mind the contempt that Mr. It. Pierpoint treated them with on Monday night, when he was asked to answer a few plain questions. The subjects alluded to are vitally affecting the homes and prosperityof War_ rington and other manufacturing centres. Why was the question of mining royalties not answered by Mr. Pier-

point? He is seeking the votes of a constituency largely composed of ironworkers. Now, it is a well known fact, that Warrington this year alone has lost many large merchant iron orders which have been sup- plied by Germany. The wire trade is in a depressed state, awing mainly to German competition. The wire nail business is in a very low state through the same causes—through exorbitant royalty rents and iniquitous way-leave payments. There has to be paid 23. 3d. per ton in England tc scl. paid on the continent. The con- sequence is that our English manufacturers cannot quote low enough to enable them to obtain orders,unless the wages of our ironworkers were cut down to mean slavery and degradation. If Mr. rierpoint does not know of these evils and unjust laws, then he is not the man for the working-class. If he ignores the subject and will not help to redress such crying evils, why the best thing for him to do is to return to Africa and be- come the Sheik of the fanatics he told his audience about, for Englishmen, I hope, will not be gulled by uch clap-trap as his.

I now pass on to Mr. Pierpoint's answer to "Are you in favour of one man, one vote ?" The answer to this question was a bit of pure evasion. The answer to "Are you prepared to use your influence to secure the payment of members of Parliament ?" was " most certainly not, as he was not willing to tax the country for work that could be done for nothing." Can we accept this answer as being genuine? I think not, and I will just show you why. Every new demand of the people is treated by the Tories first with contempt, followed by cowardice, and then concession. History proved from the time of Catholic Emancipation down to the question of Free Education, that the words conceit, contempt, coercion, corruption, cow.ardice and concession have been the very marrow of Toryism. Kindly allow me to give only one illustration of what I mean.

In 1885 Mr. Chamberlain ably advocated the principle of Free Education, and I well remember what the leading men of the Tory party said at the time. Hero is what Sir It. Cross toll his hearers at a Conservative meeting held in the Cambridge Hall, Southport, on November 20', 1885 :—" Mr. Chamberlain, a leader of the new Radical party, has brought before the country the question of Free Education, but I emphatically say that education can not be free. Somebody will have to pay for it. Schoolmasters do not grow up like mushrooms and cost nothing ; therefore someone will have to pay for these children. I do not see what right any man has to ask for his children to be taught free when he can pay for it himself. (Applause.) That principle I will always oppose." (Loud applause). Mr. Goschen speaking on the sante subject said" that greater interest was taken in schools by the parent who paid for the education of his children than by the parent who got his children's education free." Now mark the end of all this kind of opposition. Lard Cross, Mr. Goschen, and the other ministers who form the present "organised hypocrisy" have eaten all that they said, and now brag about giving what they first condemned., So we must not place any faith in what Mr. Robert Pierpoint or Mr. Rentoul says when speaking on the payment of members, or any of the other things to which they say no. For— A. Providence fashlened 'em holler

In orrler that they might their princerples swollen" Naturalists tell us that the skunk of the backwoods of America wheu being pursued emits such an awful stench that it is impossible to follow it. After going through Mr. Rentoul's speeches, I have come to tho conclusion that he is akin to that animal. His ungallant rA'erence to Mrs. Houston.the silly quibble on the pronunciation of Dr. Houston's name, the vile inuendo on Mr. Gladstone regarding the death of General Gordon,point Mr.Eentoul out as a coarse political buffoon, and a purveyor of Tory garbage. Let us hope that the electors will see the shameless- ness of these unscrupulous Tory politicians, who care nothing for truth so long as they can discredit their op- ponents.—Yours faithfully, EDWIN WRIGHT.
BRIMSTOOA.N AN' TRA.YCLE.
(MIXED.) 131 Tum o' DICK 0' Boo's.

Is id etiquette to be cheeky to a Duke ? Is id' treeason to chaff him ? BProse iv it's nayther aw should like to tawk to th' Duke o' Cambridge like a fayther. Id were nobbut th' Vother week as aw were mentionin' heaw upset aw wor abeawt th army—nod meeanin' General Booth's lot—an' especially after th' evidence gi'n bi Duke Cambridge. Wolgeley, an' others, an' th' repo3rt o' Lord Wan- tage's Committee. An neaw th' noble Duke's bin speawtin' at th' Lord Mayor's Easter banquet last I Monda' fleet, an' fairly puttin' th' cap on, an' showin heaw hi fit. To know th' pappers referred to th' army as a lot o' lads as couldn'd carry their knap- sacks—an' th' poor underfed childer may wed l nod Ibe able—sooa his Dukeship (aw fancy that's th' coourt way o' tawkin') hed a slap at th' noospapper ' chaps, an' at th' same time fished for , some " cheers," an' " Hear, hears." He geet 'em, for th' fish booat as merry as snigs an' perch bite, but he med a. bit of a—well,ne'er mind wod—ov hissel, be- cose aw'm nod so sure abea.wt th' treeason. His Dukeness wanted to know dud they want him to send in his clooas, ("No, no ") an' said other nations were armin' "to the teeth," an' we mon do th' same. That's wheere the jooak comes in. Doesn'd ta know, Duke, as eawr, men corn'd arm to th' teeth, simply becose they hevn'd cut 'em o' yet? Like th' Duke, aw'm a varra eawtspokken chap, an' mi candid opinion is as th' owd " blade " —as he kessens hissel'—is'nd as breet or as sherp as it used to be. Forther, as we ne'er shall hey a day- cent army till we heawse, an' feed, an' clooathe id, —yigh, an' pay id for werkin',isted o' batin' id woss nor weyvers is bated. Th' vulgar word is " rob " yo'r Grace. Pilate axt " wod is truth? "

_ Some fooak say id lies at th' bottom ov a well an mon ha' kickt th' bucket, but heaw's this bit ov evidence strike yo' It's fro' some proceedin's connection wi' a Conservative club at Stockport ; th' solicitor for th' defence 'ast a witness what he wor :
" A joiner and carpenter." " What did you go to the club for at five in the mccning ? " Why, what do men go to clubs for ?" " Tell me what you went for ? " "Some booze, what else?"

" You thought you would get it then ? " "I did'nt know what time it was; the clock was stopped." " Had you got sober from your booze overnight ?" Oh,yes; it does'nt take so long for me to analyse it." "Then you can analyse it in 21 hours ? " " Most decidedly; any man can who has a good constitution." This mon had bin boozed at half-past two o' th' Sunda' mornin', an' torned up at th' club at. a querter to five for moore. This is varra elevatin' an' amusin', an' id gi's me another idea for mi friend Goschen, thad is as he should mek a cherge for ad- mission to th' Ceawnty Courts, Poleece Courts, Quarter Sessions, an' Assizes, throughout th' coun- try. They're geddin' better nor Theaythers an' music halls—even on fost neet, an' iv th' Chancellor o'th' Exchequer nobbut adopts my idea he'll hey a' ten million sorplus next year at leeast. Dash id! A good laughable promise o' breeches case wod olez attract a daycent heawse at, say,prices fro thrippence i th body o' th' court to hofe a sovran for seeats aside o' th' judge ; for a divoorce case th' prices could be doubled, an' for a female pizener double 'em ageean. Th' courts wod be filled to o'er- flowin', an' as o' these different events are happenin' every day Goschen could recken on a steady revenue every year. Th' Maybrick case wod ha' browt millions i' th' way o' gate money; sooa wod th' Crawford-Dilke case, an' Mrs. Osborne's, too. An' another thing: For th' hist day o' th' trial, when sentence were bein' ony price could be gotten; ten pounds itin'd too mich forth' Aristocracy to pay for satisfyin' their curiosity', or experiencin' sensations, or hevin' th' pleasure o bein' in" at the death" o' some poor wretch. Eh, aw could welly cry when aw come to think o' th' millions an' billions o' peawnds as hes bin lost to th' country through r °body hevin' this grand idea afoore me; an' moore sooa when aw think o' th' size o' th' National debt, th' heavy-taxes, th' enormous ameawnt o' distress th' country, th' Balaclava men hevin' to go to th' werkheawse, an' things o' th' same soort, sich as literary men like Richard Jefferies deein' , poverty —yigb, an' even a paltry three years' grant to Ben Brierley o' fifty peawnd a year. For two pins aw'd put up as membero' Perlyment an' wire in gradely iv aw geet retorned. Aw'd summat else to tell yo' this week, but aw've fergetten wod id is through thinkin' o' this scheeam ; aw darsay id'll strike me bi next week, though. Onyway aw know id were varra good, an' aw, fancy id were a buzz o' some Boort ; but aw dorn'd mind fergeddin' id otogether iv Goschen teks th' hint aw've gin him.

RUNCORN v. WIDNES. A special match between these clubs, was played at Runcorn, on Wednesday evening,for the benefit of both clubs. There were about 1,500 spectators present, a heavy downfall of rain having a bad effect on the gate. In the first half Crompton dropped a coal and Davies seared a try,which Crompton converted. In the second half Widnes scored a goal from a penalty kick and Fair Turner, (Warrington), scored a try, and kicked one goal. The final result of a good game was, Runcorn two goals. (9 Points). Widnes, two goals, (8 points.)

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 30, 189.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 30, 189.

THE MELBOURNE MURDER.' RENEWED APPLICATION FOR THE POSTPONE- MENT OF THE TRIAL. WHAT DEEMING TOLD THE DOCTORS. MELBOURNE, WEDNESDAY.-At the Criminal Court here to-day, before Mr. Justice Hodges, Deeming's council, Messrs. Deakin and Forlonge, made a fresh application to have the trial of the prisoner for the Windsor murder postponed, in order that further inquiry might be made as to his mental condition.

Mr. Walsh, Crown Prosecutor, opposed the applica- tion at some length. The Jadge said—l am asked to give the doctors a further opportunity to test the prisoner's mental condi- tion. That application I will not dispose of now, but to-morrow I will hear medical evidence on both sides. I feel that my position is one of great responsibility, but the interests of the community demand that a person accused of such a crime as this should be tried immedi- ately, and if found guilty should suffer the extreme penalty of the law. If lam satisfied that a further postp3nement of the case is necessary, I will grant it ; but if the evidence on the point is not conclusive the trial must proceed. Deeming will accordingly be brought up for trial when the Court resumes to-morrow morning. In interviews which I have had with the doctors who examined Deeming, I have been informed that they , elicited from him the following among other statements : The prisoner's name as a child was Frederick Deem- ing. He remembers nothing of his life before he reached the age of twelve, except that he was sent by his father to an asylum near London. From that establishment he was taken away by his mother and was under her care between the ages of twelve and sixteen. He was never in robust health, but was nevertheless always in mis- chief. His scrapes, however, never ended in his being sent to prison. He was generally- called " Mad Fred," and one occasion, while still a boy, he threw a girl into a canal for calling him by that name. He afterwards changed his name to Harry, and when about 16 ran away to London, Where he knocked about for some time, and, having been reduced to a starving condition, he was placed in an asylum as "Teddy Williams." He did not remain there long. He climbed over the wall and got away, but was subsequently arrested while tearing his clothes to pieces in the street. He was sent to a House of Correction, whither he was traced by the chap- lain of the asylum where he had been confined. Instead of taking him back to the asylum, however, the chap- lain got him sent to sea. From early life he was in the habit of frequently changing his name, and passing from one employment to another. With regard to his family history, he states that his , father's mind was unhinged, that he was of a very violent temperament, and that he died in a lunatic asylum at Birkenhead. His mother he describes as good and kind, but she also was confined in a lunatic asylum until shortly before the prisoner's birth. His brother Sam, he asserts, was likes. ,3e confined in a lunatic asylum, but this fact was on,y known to his other brother Albert. When in England last year the prisoner declares he vainly endeavoured to ascertain the where- abouts of his brother Sam. He has a sister, who is employed as a housemaid at New Brighton, near Liver- pool, and another, who is " not right in her head." FURTHER POSTPONEMENT REFUSED. DEFENCE BRIEFS WITHDpAWN. Mr. Justice Hodges, at Melbourne. on Thursday, finally refused the application for the postponement of the trial of Deeming, and the trial was accordingly prc :teeded with. Mr. Deakin announced that Mr. Lyle, prisoners soli- citor, had withdrawn his briefs from himself and Mr. Forlonge. The latter, however, then rose, and said he would nevertheless undertake the defence, receiving his instructions from the dock.

Shortly after the expiration of the brief adjournment which followed on the refusal of Judge Hodges to grant a postponement of the trial, Deeming was placed in the dock. He was neatly dressed in a frock coat and had on a pair of buttoned boots. His beard and mous- tache have grown so much in the interval that his ap- pearance has completely changed since the inquest. In the meantime the case for the prosecution :was opened by Mr. Walsh. The witnesses for the Crown were then called, the evidence being for the most part a repetition of that tendered at the inquest. Proof was again offered of the main facts incriminating the prisoner. His passage to Melbourne with the murdered woman in the Kaiser Wilhelm, the taking of the home at Windsor, and the subsequent discovery of the body of his wife beneath the hearthstone in one of the rooms were all severally deposed to. The whole of the witnesses without hesita- tion identified the prisoner under his various aliases of Lawson, Williams, and Swanst4n. Throughout the proceedings Deeming maintained a sullen demeanour. He was constantly occupied in writ- ing notes to his counsel, and from time to time intnr- jectecl observations which were inaudible in the body of the court.

div.head: THREE LAWYERS. HAVE YOU SEEN THE SHEIK GREAT TORY PLAY AT THE PUBLIC HALL.
div.p: THE THREE LAWYERS. HAVE YOU SEEN THE SHEIK GREAT TORY PLAY AT THE PUBLIC HALL.
(BY WILFRED B. OLDING.)

The Public Hall, Warrington, was crowded on Monday evening last to witness the performance of the above play, cheap interest being centred in the fact that eloquent Reutoul from London with an extensive reperteire of Irish "bulls " would take the chief part. Previous to the commencement of the play pro- per, a new and original feature consisting of a series of transformation scenes was indulged in, and from all sides of the house this departure was evidently viewed with much satisfaction and plea- sure. In the centre of the Hall was a huge canvas covered with blue cloth, and on enquiry it was intimated that the candidate and his supporters were to be photographed during the transformation to follow. _ .

The chair was taken at 7.30 by Lawyer Davies who was supported on his right hand by Lawyer Rentoul and on his left by Lawyer Pierpoint. At the entrance end of the platform sat Parson Carleton, who scrambled into position up by the front in a manner rather wanting in dignity for so grave a representative of the party of " Law and Order." Next to him was seated Mr. T. C. London, one of the speakers of the evening, with countenance as un- movable as marble. What was troubling the gentle youth ? The wicked French nation with its want of stabilit y and general inanity " dontchernow," and a great fear had seized him lest we should be tempted to treat France other than as a door mat to wipeour feet upon. A miscellaneous mass of muddled politi- cians congregated in the rear, the organ playing for their especial benefit, " We don't want to fight (from their appearance no one would have accused them of such a dreadful propensity) "but by Jingo if we do." At the word " Jingo " their sticks, feet, and umbrellas came to the floor with a crash. The effect was charming, and added much to the enjoy- ment of the evening. And now for the transforrua- tions Transformati on 1. . The photographer, who was very nervous, and whose repeated applications to a certain small bottle excited the envy of not a few around him, had hardly time to get his apparatus in order, when up went the curtain, and there stood the three lawyers, arrayed in the legal gowns, smiling and bowing, the tall one in the centre, the small ones on each side. The photographer did his duty as be- came a loyal subject; the organ played vigorously "The three old maids of Lee;" the audience shouted itself hoarse ; and the curtain—why, the curtain fell.

Transformation 2. Lawyer Davies seated, on one side Lawyer lien- tool, clad in the robes of an Irish Doctor of Law, and on the other Lawyer Pierpoint, arrayed in the gown of an Oxford Master of Arts, both stand- ing; deafening cheers; photographer noticeably unsteady about his pins. Transformation 3. La Ryer Davies standing and gracefully enfolding his shoulders with the Union Jack. The chief per- formers seated either side 'of him. Lawyer Rentoul in the garb of an Irish peasant with an immense blackthorn across his knees, and a very small clay pipe in his mouth. Lawyer Pierpoint resplendent in the attire of a Warrington Volunteer trying the edge of a ferocious looking sword. Organ pound- ing away "We don't want to fight, &c.' Audience: pit—mad; gallery—madder; platform—clean gone. Photographer decidedly offensive in his language, threatening to " do " for one or two unlucky wights in the vicinity. Curtain—stuck fast. Transformation 4 and last ; "Every man Jack" on the platform seated astride a barrel marked with three white crosses. A huge barrel for the table. Above them a large inscrip- tion in blue and white" We support the stability of the British Empire, swearing by the name of Salisbury." Organ—" God save the Queen ;" audi- ence wildly enthusiastic : Photographer—removed by the police, collapse of the camera—several ladies' dresses spoiled. ( I Conservatives I") Then came the business ot the evening. The Chair- man, Lawyer Davies, rose, and addressed the meet- ing as follows :—Glad to be here—great meeting- -ahem—rather overpowered " dontchernow dear friend Pierpoint been to Africa—bad health good health—seen African sheik—(deafening cheers) —Warrington man—can find his way about town— jolly good fellow—not a foreigner. (Great applause, Lawyer Rentoul conspicuously energetic)—able to defend his country—a Warrington Volunteer would say no more—all want to hear eloquent Ren- toul. He then resumed his seat amid cheers. The candidate theu addressed the meeting. Glad to be here—great and • iprecedented meeting—been to Africa, had seen a sheik—had come back and meant to fight. (The platform assumed a ferocious aspect.) lie would tight (much cheering)—a volun- teer—a Warrington volunteer (great and continued cheering)—dear friend Rentoul there—their friend (Ponderous demonstration of affection by the plat- form)—would they return him? ("Yes, yes.") That I was what he left the sheik for—in voting for him 1 they voted for their own interests—their pockets. Self-complacent smile broke over the audience, and Lawyer Pierpoint sat down. All expeotant, the audience waited for eloquent Rentoul and when this mighty orator rose it was noticed that, slung on his back, was an immense album draped in blue and green. On inquiry, I found that the albund contained the portrait of the twelve hundred ladies who voted for him at his last London election. He was glad to be there—great, astounding, un- precedented meeting—many ladies there—very glad--believed in equality of sexes—in the begin- ning God made two men, one was a woman. (Great enthusiasm.) Pierpoint had seen a shiek—must return ; Pierpoint—young man a pair of trousers two inches too long—mother cut off two inches. and five sisters two inches each. , (Exhibition of mutilated pants above speakers head to the great dismay of the primrose dames). Like Liberal party, swallowed everything.—Pay members ?—No. Should he, the eloquent one, work for a .E 1 per day? (Wild shouts of "No " "No," from 18s. per week men).—Do it for the honour— Cost him 2s. 6d. per day postage. (Long faces on the platform). Ireland happy—lreland satisfied— seventeen couples reproved for flirtation in church—An Irishman worth two Englishmen. All the intelligence on their side (cheers)—knew nothing about mining royalties. Must vote for Pierpoint—he had seen a sheik—knew his way about town.—(Great applause.) I did not stay the performance out, but I have been given to understand that it gave every sat- isfaction. Everyone went away happy, though gulled.

WYCLIFFE SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY. IThe anniversary of Wycliffe Sunday School was celebrated on Sunday by special services. The morning and evening preacher was the Rev. J. K. Nuttall, of Great George-street, Liverpool, whose discourses were listened to by large congregations, the attendance in the evening being particularly numerous. There was a very large attendance of teachers, parents and scholars, at the afternoon service, at which Miss B. Dutton, of Moore, gave an address. With regard to Miss Dutton's address it is stated in" Wycliffe Church Record" for May that "her words were listened to with great delight and would long be remembered." " Miss Dutton," it is added, " has peculiar aptitude for persuasive and impressive presentation of truth, and conveys to her hearers the conviction that her sole aim is to be of service." The musical arrangements of the day were made by Mr. Geo. Wallington,as choir master, and Mr. W. H. Payton as organist. The anthems were, both morning and evening, very effectively given, the solos being taken by Mr. Ernest Booth and Miss Roberts. In the afternoon solos were sung by Miss B. Rathbone, Miss Booth and Miss M. Pay- ton, and a recitation was given by Mr. G. Lowe. The collections for the day amounted to close upon £37.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

MELBOURNE, Fainay.—The hearing of the case against Deemifig for the Windsor murder was resumed this morning. Featherston, the carrier, who conveyed the luggage belonging to the prisoner and his wife to the house at Windsor, was cross-examined as to the identity of the latter with the woman whose remains were shown to him at the morgue. He said her face was much con- tracted, but he recognised her by her auburn pair. When first asked to identify Deeming he:saw him in the gaol among twenty others. Other witnesses were then called to prove that the prisoner and his wife occupied the house at Windsor, and that about Christmas a neighbour was awakened at night by hearing curious noises a9lif carpenters' or plum- bers' work was being carried on in the dwelling-house. Alfred Spedding, another of the witnesses examined at the inquest, deposed to having found a printed card in the house on which, although the writing was almost illegible, could just be deciphered the words, " Albert Williams, commercial, Rainhill." Louisa Atkinson, another witness,was cross-examined with respect to a woman whom she said she saw about Christmas running down the lane adjoining the house in Andrew-st., Windsor, wringing her hands and cryinz. Counsel endeavoured to fix the exact date of this occu- rence, which witness gave as the 23rd or 24th of December. Witness was positive that it was one of these two days. Further evidence was then taken as to the movements Of the accused, and his assumption of various aliases, but nothing transpired to vary the facts elicited at the inquest. Miss Rounseville testified that the prisoner twice pro- posed marriage to her. The first proposal was made at Coogee, a waterside suburb of Sydney, upon the day she arrived at Sydney from Adelaide. She had met Williams under the name of Swanston on the steamer. Williams said:he would go to Bathurst and consult her sister concerning the marriage, as she did not wish to marry without her sister's consent. He went to Bathurst with her, and his second proposal was made at Bathurst. She again accepted him. On the way to Bathurst he offered her the clothing which he said had longed to his sister. She refused it, not liking the idea of wearing a dead person's things. He seemed very devoted to her, and anxious to make her happy He was kind and jolly, and said he was deeply in love with her. As far as she had seen there was no differ_ ence between his action and that of other men who were courting women whom they proposed to marry. She had returned to Williams the money sent her for her passage to West Australia. Max Hirchfield was cross-examined as to the nature of the fits from which Deeming suffered during the railway journey from Perth to Albany. According to this wit- ness the first seizure lasted a considerable time, during which it was necessary for four men to hold the accused. The secorld came on an hour and a half later, but was of briefer duration and the prisoner was much quieter. In neither fit was there any foaming at the mouth. A constable who travelled In the adjoining carriage to the prisoner deposed to the violence of his struggles whilst the seizure lasted.
I bui
1 beli

The case for the prosecution was still incomplete when the court adjourned till to-morrow. The trial will probably be concluded on Monday next Deeming's demeanour is greatly depressed, and he seems to have abandoned all possible hope. DEEMING AND JACK THE RIPPER.

div.head: ALLEGED CONFESSION.
div.p: ALLEGED CONFESSION.

MELBOURNE, THURSDAY.—The " Standard " to-day reports that the prisoner Deeming had made statements to his lawyers and to the doctors engaged on his behalf, which leave little doubt of his identity with "Jack the Ripper." The journal adds :—We think it safe to say without reserve that Williams, or Deeming, has directly confessed to having committed the majority of the ripper murders.

A WlFit's MAINTENANCE.—At the Leigh Police Court, on Monday, Peter Darwell, of Lowton, was summoned to show cause why he should not contribute towards the maintenance of his wife, who was in an asylum.—The magistrates made an order for defendant to pay 4s. per week.
PROPOSED TECHNICAL INSTITUTE FOR RUNCORN.

On Wednesday the Technical Education Com- mittee of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners de- cided to issue an appeal to the inhabitants of Run- corn for subscriptions in aid of the proposed Tech- nical Institute. The circular bears a lithogragh of the front elevation of the Institute, and the Corn- mittee state " The Building is to comprise on the ground floor a lecture hall 50 feet by 25 feet giving accommodation for from 200 to 300 persons, which can be divided by a movable partition into a school and class rooms. Also rooms for instruction in building and machine construction with a museum or model room. On the first floor, a large room for elementary drawing and class rooms for advanced drawing models and draw- ing from life. A laboratory and lecture room for experi- mental science, with the master's room, cookery room with kitchen range,&c. The basement contains rooms for work connected with the building trades and mechanics. The cost (exclusive of the site which is given by the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners) is estimated at £3,500. There being no Institution in Runcora corres- ponding to the Grammar Schools of other towns it is proposed that the large room on the ground floor should be used for the purpose of a High Grade Public School, and so supply a want that has been long and severely felt. This room would also be available for lectures in connection with the University Extension and other kindred movements. The Runcorn Improvement Com- missioners have levied a rate of id. in the £ being the largest amount they have power to raise by that means. This rate realizes about £195 per annum. The County Council for Cheshire have made a grant of £220 in aid. It is expected that this sum will be an annual one. The labove sums together with the students fees and the government grant will be required for the annual main- tenance of the Institution. The sum of £3,500 required for building the Institute must therefore be raised from other sources. A building grant will be made by the Science and Art Department the amount of which cannot exceed £l,OOO and may be contiderably less. Application has been made to the County Council for a grant in aid of the erection and it is anticipated that-a substantial sum will be received from this source. For the balance we have to appeal to the generosity of those interested in education in this district, to the gentry, and to the employers of labour. The ratepayers having taxed them- selves to the full extent allowed in support of the object and having provided the land free of charge have the greater confidence that they will not appeal in vain for assistance to those who are in a position to help. J. T. Brunner, Esq., M.P., has conditionally promised £5OO. P. Speakman, Esq., C.C., has promised £5O. The Com- mittee will gladly receive donations in aid of the building fund made payable to their treasurer, J. B. Holland Esq., Parr's Bank, Runcorn. The appeal is signed by Mr. Francis Wiswall, Chairman of the Technical Instruction Committee.
RECEPTION AT THE CONSERVATIVE
CLUB. SIR GILBERT GREENALL BIDS FAREWELL
TO HIS SUPPORTERS.

On Thursday evening, the Assembly Room, at the Warrington Conservative Club, was crowded on the occasion of a reception by Sir Gilbert Greenall, Ml'. Sir Gilbert was busy throughout the evening in an adjoining room shaking hands with those who thronged in upon him, and did not make his appearance at the more public proceedings. Mr. John White, president of the Conservative Assooia- tion, presidcd at the former part of the proceedings, and Alderman Francomb, vice-president, of the as- sociation took the chair during the latter part, there being also present on the platform, Lady Greenall, the Misses Greenall, Mr. Gilbert Greenall, Mr. T. W. Legh,.M.P., Mr. R. Pierpoint, Aluermen Fran- comb, Sutton, and Wright. Mr. John WHIT's read a letter from Mr. J. C. Parr from abroad, expressing regret at his inability to be home in time for the reception ; and at the occasion of the meeting. The memory of Sir Gilbert Greenall, lie zemarked, would be cherished as that of a worthy re- presentative of the good old town of Warrington ; and he expressed the hope that his successor would emulate his example, and that Warrington would remain as true to her colours for the next 50 years as it had done. Mr.„l White expressed on behalf of Sir Gilbert his regret that he was not able to take a more active part in the pro- ceedings, and the pleasure it gave him to be amongst them. Referring to remarks by Mr. Jahn Rylands and other Liberal speakers, Mr. White said they seemed to think that now Skr Gilbert Greenall was retiring Greenallism was dead. He thought that if they had been there that night they would have had ample proof that the spirit of Greenallism still lived. (Applause.) The opposite side were making a great mistake in laving the flattering unction to their souls that because Sir Gilbert was retiring they were going to have a very easy walk over. He thought they would find that the reverse would happen—(applause)—and the very fact of losing Sir Gilbert would make the Con- ' servatives all the more determined to preserve them- selves in that united condition in which they had always be while he had been at their head. The Speaker institu- ted comparisons between Sir Gilbert as their grand old man, and Mr. Gladstone as the Liberal grand old man. In one respect, lie said, they were alike—in having been in Parliament longer than anybody except Mr, Villiers of Wolverhampton. But Mr. Gladstone bad represented- some six or seven constituences and been gradually turned out of one after another. Sir Gilbert had always represented but one constituency. (Applause.) Then again he was given to understand that Mr. Gladstone was born in at least six different places—(laughter) —Sir Gilbert was only born in one place—Wilderspoot Sir Gilbert commenced his political life as a Conserva- tive, and so he had remained, and always would remain. The other grand old man commenced life as a Conservative also, and afterwards became a Liberal; then a Radical, then a Parnellite. He would simply make this remark that lie believed a golden opportunity was about to be presented to the Warrington Conserva- tives, and he trusted that when the time arrived they would avail themselves of it to the best possible advan- tage. (Applause.) Mr. T. W. Lana, M.P., afterwards addressed the meeting. He expressed his pleasure at being present at such an interesting ceremony, which, the occasion being one where an aged and deeply respected gentleman bade farewell to political life, to his fellow-citizens, and to the borough which he had so long represented, appealed to the sympathies of everyone. (Applause.) He sincerely and devoutly wished that his political end might be as peaceful as Sir Gilbert's appeared to be. (Applause.) Mr. Legh, referring to Dr. Houston, said so far as he was able to see that gentleman relied for getting into Parlia- ment upon the vocal talents of his wife. (Laughter.) If he was not mistaken Dr. Houston was endeavouring to get himself sung into Parliament. Ile was not alto- gether surprised that Mrs. Houston's songs met with conspicuous success as compared with Dr. Houston's speeches. His statements were so remarkable that he could not refrain from alluding to them. He said among other things that if you bestowed Horse Rule upon Ireland the trade of the country would revive and the Irish would send a vast amount of raw products into this country. Ile (Mr. Legh) was convinced that the first thing Ireland would do would be to put on strong pro-, tective duties ; and the only products which would find their way to this country would be those of the same quality as Dr. Houston, a product for which there was no particular demand in this.country, and which might possibly be returned to its purveyor in a more or less damaged condition. (Laughter.) Mr. R. PIERPOINT who was received with enthu- siasm, was the succeeding speaker. He said it must be an exceedingly gratifying ihing for Sir Gilbert to look back upon se long and so faithful a service as he could do. 'His Parliamentary career began in 1847, and be sat till 1868, and but for the unfor- tunate mistake of a polling clerk he would have continued to sit, but he was elected again in 1874 and sat till 1880, and then again from 1885 to the present moment. He had had a very long, and he was sure they would believe with him, a very creditable career. (Ap- plause.) He had seen It great succession of administra- tions, those of Lord John Russell, Lord Derby, Lord Aberdeen, Lord Palmerston, and Mr. Disraeli, and, now, the Marquis of Salisbury. Alderman SUTTON, hon.isecretary of the Conservative Association, after accounting for the absence of Mr. W. H. Bleckley and other gentlemen, made some remarks on the occasion. He entered into some reminiscences of one of Sir Gilbert's early canvasses,and said he was very much amused at his kissing all the young ladies he came near in his canvass. He expressed the beliel that if Sir Gilbert could put up again every Conservative in War- ringten would vote for him. (Applause.) He also ex- pressed his regret that Sir Albert Rollet's bill had not been passed, because he believed there were so many Conservative ladies, who took such interest in politics, as provod by that meeting, that if they all had votes the Conservative majority in Warrington would be very much increased. He had not the slightest doubt that they would have votes before long, and when that time came they would be in a verytnuch safer position than at present, though they were in quite good enough posi- tion at any time to meet any Irishman. (Applause.) Alderman FRANCOMB proposed a resolution congratu- lating Lord Winmarleigh on having attained his 90th birthday. Mr. John FAIRCLOOGIC seconded, and it was carried.

Mr. LONDON afterwards addressed the meeting. The speeches were interspersed with songs by Miss Newcombe, and songs and recitations by Mr. Duncan Liverpool, who gave great satisfaction. Mr. Wm. John_, son accompanied the songs. "God Save the Queen " sung to the accompaniment of Mr. John White, concluded the meeting. Refreshments were provided below stairs for the visitors.

SHOCKING FATALITY.-9n Friday afternoon, as a num- ber of children were playing on the high road at Horns Smithy,Huyton, one of them named Jas. F. H. Dilworth ran after a lorry belonging to Ann Wilson, carrier, St. Helens. His foot caught in the spokes of the wheel, and before the horse could be stopped the boy was carried round with the wheel and killed, the body being dread- fully mangled.
