A RACEHORSE POISONED. The Duke of Westminster's statement that Orme has been poisoned will be investigated by the police.
ARREST OF ANARCHISTS IN FRANCE. PARIS, FRIDAY AFTsutiool4.—Three Anarchists were arrested at Choisy Le Roy to-day. -DEATH OF SIR ALBXANDER ACLAND HOOD. _ _

Sir Alexander Acland Hood, Bart., died yesterday from pneumonia, aged 73. He was formerly Conservative member for West Somerset, and his son, who succeeds to the title, is the prcsent Unionist candidate for the same constituency. THE COTTON LOCK-OUT.
The lock-out in the cotton trade is being very severely felt at Heywood, where only 1,000 out of 3,000 opera- tives are receiving aid from the trade. societies.

The Bolton master cotton spinners decided yes to run only four days a week. This decision will affect 20,000 operatives. CHARGE OF KILLING A MOTHER. A young man named Hearn was arrested on Thursday night, on a charge of killing his mother, at her home at revercene, about five miles from Waterford. Hearn was brought before the magistrates yesterday asternoon and committed for trial charged with manslaugter. It is alleged thal he treated the deceased cruelly, and eventually knocked her down and kicked her till she was unconscions. She lingered two days, and then suc- cumbed.

STORM AND WRECK. A heavy gale sprang up at an early hour on Thursday morning, and prevailed with varying strength until tha afternoon. Coasting steamers arriving in the Mersey reported very heavy weather outside. During the height of the gale off the Tyne a salmon fishing boat was seen to disappear, and another boat is missing. Four vessels are aground south of Drogheda Bay. During the gale the Scarborough life-boat rescued the crew of the yawl Margaret off the port. Another fishing boat, the Unity, had not made the harbour on Thursday night, and it is feared she has gone down witb four hands. On Thursday night two bodies ware washed ashore at Sunderland, and they have been identified as those of Isaac Chattam and William Clark, North Shields fisher- men, who put off in a boat to seek their friends during the storm, and were drowned.

YESTERDUE'S PARLIAMENT. -- HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Deputy Speaker (Mr. Courtney), in the continued absence of the Speaker owing to indisposition, took the chair at ten minutes past three o'clock. NOTICES OF MOTION.—Sir E. Birkbeck gave notice that this day four weeks he will call attention to the need for increased postal facilities In rural parishes. Colonel Howard Vincent gave notice that he will call attention this day four weeks to the amount of old age pauperism in this country. MRS. MONTAGUE'S PRISON DRESS.— Dr. Tanner asked the Chief Secretary for Ireland whether he wouln state ' point blank whether Mrs. Montague was wearing the ordinary prison dress. Mr. Jackson read the prison rule, and stated that application had been made to the Prisons Board on behalf of Mrs. Montagu, and the Board saw no reason to make any exception in her case. (Cheers and laughter.) THE COURSE OF BUSINESS.—Mr. BALFOUR moved a re- solution appropriating morning sittings on Tuesdays and Fridays for Government business. Mr. H. Gardner and Mr. Macartney followed the leader of the House. Sub- sequently Mr. GLADSTONI rose and protested against the management of business by Ministers. They ought to be very well aware that the Opposition was anxious to get forward with the Small Holdings Bill, but they were putting off dis- cussion and settlement until the last moment. Mr. BALFOUR said the Local Government Bill would be taken in the middle of May at the very best period of the session. The resolution was eventually agreed to without a division. HOME RULE ALL ROUND. On the motion to go into Committee ot Supply Dr. Ccarixe, moved a -rosolution setting forth the desirability of legislative assembles in Ireland, Scotland, Wales, and England having the management and control of domes- tic affairs. Mr. Shaw Stewart contended that the attendance of representatives in such assemblies would tend to diminish or destroy the proper influence and control over imperial legislation. R. T. Reid supported the resolution.
On the House dividing. after considerable discussion, the resolution was lost by 74 to 54.

div.head: ALLEGED BIGAMY AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: ALLEGED BIGAMY AT ST. HELENS.

On Tuesday, at St. Helens Police Court, James Harrison, a sinker, living at 71,Ha11-st., was charged on his own confession with committing bigamy. Chief Constable Wood stated that at half-past ten that forenoon the prisoner visited the Police Office, and made the following statement :—" I have come to give myself up on a charge of bigamy. I married Mary Ellen Wilson at Billinge Church, in January, 1890,know- mg at the time that my wife, Mary Elizabeth, whom I married at Eccleston Church, in lingust,lB73, was alive, and she is still living. I saw her in St. Helens a few days ago. I lived with my wife from 1873 to January, 1850, when she left me after selling everything in the house. I don't know where Seth Marlow and Hannah Bold live. We picked them up at Billings on our way to the church, and they were witnesses to our marriage." —The Chief Constable asked for the prisoner to be re- manded until next Monday.—Mr. J. 0. Smith, who ap- peared for the prisoner, stated that he was consulted by his client some time am). His wish was to surrender himself and take his trial on the charge of bigamy, and suffer such punishment as might be meted out to him. He had not been pressed or threatened by either of the women, and his appearance at the court was entirely of his own accord. He asked for the prisoner to be ad- mitted to bail during the remand.—The Bench granted both applieations, bail being fixed at himself in LIO and two sureties of £5 each.
- DEATH OF A WARRINOTONIAN IN

AMERICA. IMPOSING FUNERAL OF THE DECEASED. I New Bedford, Massachusetts, U.S., newspaper records the death at New Bedford, about a fort- night since,of Mr. John P. Kelley, a native of War- rington, under very melancholy circumstances. The deceased who was employed at the Washing- ton glass works, New Bedford, was a member of the fire brigade of that town, and when called out with the brigade on an alarm of fire, he jumped from the footboard of the engine, on which he had been standing. He fell, and was run over by one of the hind wheels of the engine, though every care was used,when his danger was seen,to prevent the accident. The poor man was taken home, and died soon after, his back being broken. The New Bedford paper says" he was a general favourite, and the boys [referring to the firemen] feel deeply his untimely removal." Hie funeral took place on the following Sunday, at the Roman Catholic Cemetery, about 2000. persons be- ing present, the ent‘ire fire department escorting the remains to the grave, and the fire alarm bell be- ing tolled for the occasion. Wreaths were placed on the grave by the local Glasscutters' Association, of which the deceased was president, by the Board of Engineers, and by a Fire Brigade; and there cem to have been universal signs of mourning. The record from which we quote is accompanied by a pretty fair portrait of the deceased. Mr. Kelley served his apprenticeship with Messrs. Bolton and Sons, glasscutters of this town, and resided in Jones's-buildings, Watkin-st. He emigrated to America about ten years ago, and there married a German wife, who has survived him.

CALIFORNIAN FRESIi FRUIT.—A Now Igvoriv.—An experiment of great importance is to be made with a view of introducing into this country in fresh condition the choicest Californian fruits, such as cherries, straw- berries, peaches, apricots, oranges, apples, tomatoes ; the promoters of this scheme are the Californian Fruit Transportation Company of Chicago, who undertake by means of their patent refrigerater system to land the fruit in perfect condition and so sanguine are they of this that arrangements have been made for the conveyance of large quantities weekly by the famous steamers of the White Star Line, the disposal and distribution being entrusted to Messrs. James Adam, Son and Company, of Liverpool, and Messrs. J. J. Adam and Company of London. The first shipment will be by the" Majestic" due in Liverpool en Wednesday next and the result of the experiment is anxiously looked for by those interested particularly by the shippers who desire to offer to the Zritish public the fruits of this sunny clime.

CROWNING OF THE MAY QUEEN AT GOL- BORNE. The CROWNING of th MAY QUEEN will take place on the Recreation Ground. GoThorne, on SATURDAY, MAY 7th, 1892. A GRAND PROCESSION of over 1.000 children, re- presenting different nations, trades, and characters, will leave the above Ground at 2 30. and parade the principal streets. The Queen will be crowned at 430 p.m., after which' will be performed on the ground the May Pole dance, the gypsy dance, also a special dance by the Hindley Green. mortis dancers (specially engaged). Special engagement Of the BROTHERS YELVARS. Flying Kings and Funny Acro- batic Clowns. Three Bands in attendance: playing for danc- ing until dusk. Teas and Refreshments provided on the Ground at Reasonable charges. Special accommodation for Cyclists on the Ground. Mr. Holden's "World's Fair" (in- cluding all kinds of Fun and Amusements) will be held on the Ground. Special trains will be run. For further parti- culars see large Posters. Admission. 6d. ; Enclosure, 6d. extra ; vehicles, Is. each. JOSEPH SANKEY, Secretary.

AYDOCK MAY DAY FESTIVAL. The above will take place SATURDAY, MAY 7TH, 1892. in the HAYDOCK FOOTBALL FIELD, adjoining the Wagon Hotel. I PROCESSION will leave the field at 2.15 p.m., and parade the Village, returning for the CORONATION C aREIVIONY at 4.15 p.m. A trained set of DANCERS will plait the MAY POLE. Various SPORT:. will be hold during the day, and RIGGERS will perform at intervals. HAYDOCK BRASS BAND will play for dancing till dusk. Admission to the Field. 6d. After 6 o'clook, 3d. Application for space for Stalls to be made to E. BRADSHAW, Hon. Sac.

THISTLETHWAITE. -- 322, Leeds Road, Bradford, January 15, 1892. Gentlemen,—/ have two of your Marsh's Patent Smoke consuming and Fuel-economising Fires at work continuously in my establishment. One tire has been fixed for fourteet months, working two large ovens (one heavy cast iron and one sheet iron), and the other is applied to a complete bakers range, with large ovens, side boiler, and hot plate, and they have both given every satisfaction. After getting the fires well started with nuts, we use practically nothing but smudge on the two-decker, and nuts and smudge on the range, for the remainder of the day. The heat obtained from this inferioi coal with this Patent fire is really marvellous ; indeed, one can hirdly realise tfie fact of being able to bake bread and pastry with common smudge.
